lessons.title: What JavaScript is and where it runs
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 1: What JavaScript is and where it runs

theory.contentHtml:
You open the company dashboard, switch the filter to the latest quarter, and the chart redraws right in front of you - the code handling that click is JavaScript. This lesson answers two questions before you write any code: what JavaScript is, and why someone who works with data should spend time on it.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. What JavaScript is
  2. Why data people need JavaScript
  3. What this course teaches and what it does not
  4. Run your first line of code
  5. Key points

1. What JavaScript is

JavaScript is a programming language born in 1995 for one purpose: running inside the web browser. To this day it is the only language every browser understands out of the box - Chrome, Firefox, and Safari each ship with a JavaScript engine, nothing to install.

The important turn came in 2009: Node.js took that engine out of the browser, and since then JavaScript runs anywhere - servers, personal machines, command-line tools. The result is one language, two environments:

  • In the browser - where JavaScript drives the web pages users see.
  • Outside the browser (Node) - where JavaScript works like Python: reading files, calling APIs, processing data, running servers.

For a beginner, the thing to remember is: the syntax you learn in this course works in both environments. Variables, data types, functions, loops - write them once, they run the same everywhere.

2. Why data people need JavaScript

You do not need JavaScript to run a SQL query or train a model. But everyday data work touches JavaScript more often than you might think:

  • Company dashboards are web apps. Metabase, Superset, Looker, Tableau on the web - the display layer is all JavaScript. Whenever you wonder why a chart renders the way it does, or want to embed a dashboard into an internal page, you are standing in JavaScript territory.
  • APIs return JSON. JSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation - the world's most common data format is literally JavaScript's object syntax. No language reads JSON more naturally.
  • JavaScript notebooks already exist. Observable is a data notebook like Jupyter, but the language is JavaScript - the visualization community uses it heavily.
  • The strongest charting libraries live here. D3, Chart.js, ECharts - when a static matplotlib chart is not enough and you need real interactivity, the destination is a JavaScript library.
  • Your engineering colleagues write JavaScript. Being able to read the web team's code lets you answer "where is this number computed" yourself, instead of waiting for someone to be free.

In short: SQL and Python process data, while JavaScript is where data gets seen. Know all three and you can travel from the database to the user's screen without stopping halfway.

3. What this course teaches and what it does not

This course teaches JavaScript as a data-processing tool: variables, data types, strings, arrays, objects, functions, loops, and data transformations - the things you use to compute, filter, aggregate, and format numbers.

This course does not teach:

  • The DOM and user interfaces - no buttons, forms, or page effects. That is frontend work, outside a data person's goals at this stage.
  • Asynchronous programming - no async, no API calls inside lessons. That topic needs solid fundamentals first.

The boundary is deliberate: learn the core of the language properly first, and the rest becomes much easier to pick up when you actually need it.

4. Run your first line of code

Every lesson and exercise in this course runs right inside your browser - no Node install, no terminal. Any code block with a Run button is live: click it and see the result below.

The command you will use most across the whole course is console.log - it prints a value to the console. Try it now:

console.log("hello, data");

Click Run and you see:

hello, data

JavaScript is also a calculator on the spot. For example, average order value from two numbers:

const orders = 128;
const revenue = 45600000;
console.log(revenue / orders);
356250

The first two lines declare variables - the subject of the next lesson. For now, just click Run and get comfortable with the loop edit code → Run → read the result: that is how you will learn throughout this course.

Key points

JavaScript runs in two places: inside the browser and outside it via Node.js. The core syntax you learn in this course is identical in both environments.

Data people meet JavaScript at the display layer of data - dashboards, JSON from APIs, Observable notebooks, charting libraries like D3/Chart.js. SQL and Python process data; JavaScript is where data gets seen.

This course teaches only the core language for data work - no DOM, no UI, no async. The sandbox runs right in your browser; click Run and see the result.

lessons.title: Variables let, const - and why not var
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 2: Variables let, const - and why not var

theory.contentHtml:
A variable gives a value a name so you can reuse it: this month's revenue, yesterday's order count, the current tax rate. JavaScript has three keywords for declaring variables - const, let, var - but you only need two of them, and you should understand why the third was left behind.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Declaring variables with const
  2. When to use let
  3. var is legacy
  4. Naming variables
  5. Key points

1. Declaring variables with const

const declares a variable and assigns its value exactly once:

const region = "North";
const taxRate = 0.08;
console.log(region);
console.log(taxRate);
North
0.08

The structure is always: const + variable name + = + value. From that line on, using the name anywhere gives you the value.

const is short for constant. Reassigning a const variable is an immediate error:

const taxRate = 0.08;
taxRate = 0.1; // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.

That may sound restrictive, but it is exactly the strength: most values in a piece of analysis should not change after being set - the region name, the tax rate, the raw data you read in. Declare them with const, and if some line accidentally overwrites one, JavaScript fails right at the faulty line instead of letting a silently drifted number crawl into your report.

Hence the convention of this course (and of most JavaScript teams today): default to const.

2. When to use let

let declares a variable that may be reassigned. Use it when the value genuinely needs to change while the program runs - the classic case is an accumulator:

let totalRevenue = 0;
totalRevenue = totalRevenue + 45600000;
totalRevenue = totalRevenue + 38200000;
console.log(totalRevenue);
83800000

totalRevenue starts at 0 and takes in each region's revenue - it must change, so it must be let.

The decision rule is short: write const first, and switch to let only when the runtime complains about reassignment. As a bonus, every let in your code becomes a signal to the reader: "this variable will change - keep an eye on it".

3. var is legacy

Before 2015, JavaScript only had var. It still works - you will meet it in old code and old examples online - but it carries two silently buggy behaviors that let/const fixed.

First: hoisting. A var variable is "lifted" to the top of its scope, so reading it before the declaration line does not fail - it returns undefined:

console.log(discountRate);
var discountRate = 0.05;
undefined

Run it yourself - no error at all. That undefined travels straight into whatever calculation comes next. The same code with let stops right at the faulty line:

console.log(discountRate); // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'discountRate' before initialization
let discountRate = 0.05;

Second: no block scope. A var declared inside a { } block still exists outside it:

if (true) {
  var leakedTotal = 500;
}
console.log(leakedTotal);
500

leakedTotal was created inside the if block yet remains readable outside - the variable "leaks" into a wider scope than where it was born. With let/const, a variable lives only inside its block; reading it from outside is an immediate ReferenceError:

if (true) {
  let scopedTotal = 500;
}
console.log(scopedTotal); // ReferenceError: scopedTotal is not defined

Both behaviors share the same danger: being wrong without saying so. So the course rule is short: never write var in new code; when you meet var in old code, read it as a loose version of let.

4. Naming variables

Variable names are free documentation for whoever reads the code - including you, three months from now. Three rules:

  • English, meaningful: the name says what the variable holds.
  • camelCase: first letter lowercase, each following word capitalized - totalRevenue, orderCount.
  • Avoid ambiguous abbreviations: qty is guessable, but nobody knows whether dt means date, data, or delta.

A direct comparison - the snippet below runs correctly, but nobody understands it:

const x = 45600000;
const dt = 128;
const tmp = x / dt;
console.log(tmp);

The same calculation with decent names explains itself, no comment needed:

const totalRevenue = 45600000;
const orderCount = 128;
const averageOrderValue = totalRevenue / orderCount;
console.log(averageOrderValue);
356250

Key points

Default to const; use let only when reassignment is needed. Write const first and switch when you truly must - every remaining let becomes a "this variable will change" signal.

Never write var in new code. Hoisting returns undefined instead of failing, and variables leak out of blocks - two kinds of silent bugs that let/const stop right at the faulty line. You still need to read var in old code.

Variable names: English, meaningful, camelCase. averageOrderValue explains itself; tmp forces the reader to reverse-engineer the whole block.

lessons.title: Data types numbers, strings, booleans, and the two empty ones
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 4: Data types numbers, strings, booleans, and the two empty ones

theory.contentHtml:
Working with data means working with types: is this column a number or a string, and in which sense is that cell empty. JavaScript has fewer basic types than you might expect - and one famous historical trap sits right inside this lesson.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. number - one numeric type
  2. string - text data
  3. boolean - true or false
  4. null and undefined
  5. Checking types with typeof
  6. Key points

1. number - one numeric type

If you are used to pandas with its separate int64 and float64, JavaScript is simpler: there is a single number type for both integers and decimals:

const unitPrice = 259000;
const quantity = 3;
console.log(unitPrice * quantity);
console.log(10 / 4);
777000
2.5

777000 and 2.5 are both number. Division returns the decimal part directly - there is no integer division silently cutting off the remainder like in some other languages.

Under the hood, number is a 64-bit floating-point value - exactly the float64 you know from pandas. Which means it inherits the familiar limitation of floats:

console.log(0.1 + 0.2);
0.30000000000000004

This is not a JavaScript bug - Python prints the same tail for 0.1 + 0.2, because both use the same 64-bit float standard. The practical lesson: never compare two computed decimals for exact equality, and when printing currency or percentages, format the number first - the tool for that comes in a later lesson.

2. string - text data

string is the text type: product names, region codes, order IDs. Wrap it in double quotes "..." or single quotes '...' - this course consistently uses double quotes:

const productName = "Wireless Mouse";
console.log(productName);
console.log(productName.length);
Wireless Mouse
14

.length counts characters - spaces included. One thing data people must keep in mind: "128" (a string) and 128 (a number) are two values of different types. Data read from CSV or JSON often arrives as strings, and arithmetic on numeric-looking strings produces surprising results - the template literals lesson has a concrete example.

3. boolean - true or false

boolean has exactly two values: true and false. It usually comes out of a comparison:

const revenue = 45600000;
const target = 50000000;
const reachedTarget = revenue >= target;
console.log(reachedTarget);
false

All data-filtering logic - "which orders exceed 50 million", "which customers have not activated" - stands on booleans. The comparison operators (>, <, >=, <=, ===) will be used heavily from the conditionals module onward.

4. null and undefined

JavaScript has two ways to represent "no value", and telling them apart is a real data-reading skill:

  • null - intentionally empty. The code's author deliberately assigns null to say "this cell is empty, and I know it". The exact role of NULL in SQL: an order with no assigned manager has null in that field.
  • undefined - not assigned yet. A variable that was declared but never given a value, or an access to something that does not exist. It usually signals an omission, not an intention.
let assignedManager = null;
let shippingDate;
console.log(assignedManager);
console.log(shippingDate);
null
undefined

assignedManager is empty because we said so; shippingDate is empty because nobody touched it. When inspecting API data: null means the source system confirms there is no value; undefined (or a missing field entirely) usually means the data was never written. Two different stories, leading to two different treatments.

5. Checking types with typeof

typeof returns the name of a value's type, as a string:

console.log(typeof 42);
console.log(typeof "revenue");
console.log(typeof true);
console.log(typeof undefined);
console.log(typeof null);
number
string
boolean
undefined
object

The first four lines are what you would expect. The last line is the most famous trap in JavaScript: typeof null returns "object", not "null". It is a bug from the very first version in 1995; by the time it was noticed, too many websites depended on the behavior, so the standards committee decided to keep it forever rather than break the old web.

The practical consequence: do not use typeof to check for null. To know whether a value is null, compare directly: value === null.

Key points

JavaScript has a single number type - integers and decimals alike, a float64 underneath just like in pandas. The 0.1 + 0.2 tail is a property of floats in every language, not a JavaScript quirk.

null is intentionally empty (like NULL in SQL); undefined means not assigned. Seeing null in data - the source confirms there is no value; seeing undefined - most likely nothing was ever written.

typeof null returns "object" - a historical bug kept forever. Check for null with a direct comparison value === null, never through typeof.

The string "128" and the number 128 are different types. CSV/JSON data often arrives as strings - check the type before doing arithmetic.

lessons.title: Template literals and console.log
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 6: Template literals and console.log

theory.contentHtml:
Analysis results almost always end as a line of text: "Region North: 128 orders". This lesson teaches how to weave numbers into strings cleanly - and this is exactly the toolkit you will use for every exercise in the course.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Joining strings with plus
  2. Template literals
  3. console.log with multiple arguments
  4. Formatting numbers with toFixed
  5. Key points

1. Joining strings with plus

The primitive way to combine strings and variables is the + operator:

const region = "North";
const orders = 128;
console.log("Region " + region + ": " + orders + " orders");
Region North: 128 orders

It works, but look closely: four + signs, three pairs of quotes, and every space has to be positioned by hand inside the string fragments. The longer the sentence, the easier it is to lose a space or leave a stray quote.

Worse, + has two meanings - numeric addition and string concatenation - and JavaScript decides left to right:

console.log("Total: " + 128 + 20);
Total: 12820

"Total: " + 128 produces the string "Total: 128", then + 20 concatenates into "Total: 12820" - not 148 as a quick glance suggests. This is the string-versus-number trap from the previous lesson coming back, and reason enough to use better syntax.

2. Template literals

A template literal wraps the string in backticks - the key in the top-left corner of the keyboard, next to the 1 key, not to be confused with a single quote - and embeds values with ${...}:

const region = "North";
const orders = 128;
console.log(`Region ${region}: ${orders} orders`);
Region North: 128 orders

The whole sentence is one continuous string; wherever a value belongs, you open ${ - reading the code is almost like reading the finished sentence, with every space exactly where you see it.

Inside ${...} you can put any expression, not just a variable name:

const revenue = 45600000;
const orders = 128;
console.log(`Average order value: ${revenue / orders} VND`);
Average order value: 356250 VND

From this lesson onward, the course convention is: string building means template literals. The + operator keeps exactly one job - adding numbers.

3. console.log with multiple arguments

console.log accepts multiple arguments, separated by commas, and prints them separated by a space:

const region = "North";
const revenue = 45600000;
console.log("region:", region, "revenue:", revenue);
region: North revenue: 45600000

This form is fast to type and great for inspecting values while hunting a bug - label each variable and scan the line. When the output must match a predefined format exactly (as in the exercises), a template literal gives you control over every character.

4. Formatting numbers with toFixed

Numbers coming out of a calculation often carry a long decimal tail - mathematically correct, but unfit for a report:

const orders = 128;
const visits = 3450;
const conversionRate = (orders / visits) * 100;
console.log(conversionRate);
console.log(`Conversion rate: ${conversionRate.toFixed(2)}%`);
3.710144927536232
Conversion rate: 3.71%

.toFixed(n) rounds to exactly n decimal places. .toFixed(2) for currency and percentages, .toFixed(0) when only whole numbers are wanted.

One detail worth knowing: .toFixed returns a string, not a number - its job is producing a display form (which is how it can keep trailing zeros like "3.70"). So it is the last step before printing: finish the math on numbers, then toFixed for presentation.

Key points

Build strings with template literals - backticks plus ${...}, expressions welcome. The + operator with strings walks into traps like "Total: " + 128 + 20 printing 12820.

console.log with multiple arguments prints them space-separated - the quick form for inspecting variables. When every character of the format matters, use a template literal.

.toFixed(n) rounds to n decimal places and returns a string - it is the final presentation step; never feed its result back into calculations.

This trio - constants, template literals, console.log - is the toolkit for every exercise in this course. You will use it in the very next lesson.

questions.prompt: Where does JavaScript run, and why does that matter for data work?

options.label: A
options.text: Only in the browser - running it on a server means rewriting in another language

options.label: B
options.text: In the browser and also outside it via Node.js; dashboards, Observable notebooks, and charting libraries are all JavaScript environments

options.label: C
options.text: Only on servers - browsers need a special plugin to run JavaScript

options.label: D
options.text: Inside the database engine, replacing SQL for queries

questions.explanation: JavaScript was born in 1995 to run in the browser, and browsers still understand it out of the box - no plugin needed. Since 2009, Node.js has taken the engine outside the browser, so writing JavaScript for servers is everyday reality; nobody has to rewrite it in another language. One language, two environments, the same core syntax. For data people, the concrete touchpoints sit at the display layer of data: web dashboards like Metabase/Superset/Looker, JSON - which is literally JavaScript's object syntax, Observable notebooks, and charting libraries like D3/Chart.js/ECharts. Inside the database engine, however, JavaScript does not replace SQL: querying is still SQL's job, while JavaScript sits on the processing and display side of the results.

questions.prompt: Following the course convention, how do you choose between const and let when declaring a new variable?

options.label: A
options.text: Always use let for flexibility; const is only for mathematical constants like PI

options.label: B
options.text: Default to const; switch to let only when the variable genuinely needs to be reassigned

options.label: C
options.text: const for numbers, let for strings

options.label: D
options.text: The two keywords are equivalent; pick whichever you like

questions.explanation: The rule from the variables lesson: write const first, and switch to let only when the runtime complains about reassignment. This protects values that should not change - region names, tax rates, raw input data - because an accidental overwrite fails right at the faulty line instead of a silently drifted number crawling into a report; and every remaining let in the code becomes a signal to the reader that the variable will change. The two keywords are therefore anything but equivalent: const forbids reassignment, let allows it, and the "flexibility" of let is exactly what should be limited rather than a reason to make it the default. The choice also has nothing to do with data types - const is for every assign-once value, number or string alike, not just mathematical constants like PI.

questions.prompt: Why should new code avoid var?

options.label: A
options.text: var runs slower than let, hurting performance

options.label: B
options.text: var was removed from modern JavaScript; code containing var no longer runs

options.label: C
options.text: var is hoisted and has no block scope: reading the variable before its declaration returns undefined instead of failing, and variables declared inside a block leak outside - two kinds of silent, hard-to-find bugs

options.label: D
options.text: var cannot store numbers larger than one million

questions.explanation: The two behaviors of var share one danger: being wrong without saying so. Hoisting means console.log(discountRate) placed before var discountRate = 0.05 prints undefined and the program keeps running, the empty value flowing into whatever calculation comes next - the same code with let stops immediately with a ReferenceError, pointing at the exact faulty line. The lack of block scope means a variable declared inside { } still exists outside it, living wider than its author intended. This is a matter of scoping rules, not performance - var does not run slower than let. Nor has it been removed from the language: var is still valid and runs fine (the lesson has a runnable var block); it is discouraged, not deleted, because deleting it would break millions of old websites. And a limit like "cannot store numbers above one million" simply does not exist - number safely stores values up to about 2^53, regardless of the declaration keyword.

questions.prompt: In an order record, what is the correct distinction between null and undefined?

options.label: A
options.text: They are the same value, just written differently

options.label: B
options.text: undefined is the value you deliberately assign to mark an empty field; null is what the engine produces for unassigned variables

options.label: C
options.text: null is intentionally empty, assigned by the author - like NULL in SQL; undefined is a variable that was declared but never given a value

options.label: D
options.text: null only works with numbers, undefined only works with strings

questions.explanation: null is an active statement: the author assigns it to say "this cell is empty, and I know it" - the exact role of NULL in SQL, like an order with no assigned manager having null in assignedManager. undefined, by contrast, is the default state of something nobody touched: a declared-but-unassigned variable, or a field that does not exist - so casting undefined as the "deliberate marker" swaps the two roles exactly backwards. They are not one value written two ways either: these are genuinely distinct values, and even typeof returns different results for them ("object" versus "undefined"); both can also be assigned to any variable, with no restriction tying null to numbers or undefined to strings. When inspecting API data the distinction pays off: null means the source system confirms there is no value, while undefined usually means the data was never written.

options.label: A
options.text: undefined and null

options.label: B
options.text: undefined and object

options.label: C
options.text: object and object

options.label: D
options.text: The second line throws an error because discount was never assigned

questions.explanation: let discount; declares the variable without assigning it, so discount holds undefined and typeof discount returns the string "undefined" - once a variable is declared, reading it is perfectly fine, and nothing in this snippet throws (unlike reading a let variable *before* its declaration line). typeof null, meanwhile, is the language's most famous trap: it returns "object", not "null" - a bug from the 1995 original, kept forever by the standards committee because fixing it would break the old web. Picking the pair undefined and null means trusting typeof null to return "null" - exactly what the trap punishes; the pair object and object fails on the first half, since an unassigned variable is undefined, not object. The practical takeaway: checking for null must be a direct comparison value === null, never typeof.

options.label: A
options.text: ${product}: ${price * qty} VND - the string is printed literally

options.label: B
options.text: Laptop: 50000000 VND

options.label: C
options.text: Laptop: 25000000 VND - the multiplication inside the string is ignored

options.label: D
options.text: A syntax error - you cannot put arithmetic inside a string

questions.explanation: The string is wrapped in backticks, so this is a template literal: each ${...} is evaluated and embedded into the string. ${product} becomes Laptop, and ${price * qty} is a full expression - 25000000 times 2 gives 50000000 - so the printed line is Laptop: 50000000 VND. Inside ${...} you can put any expression, not just a variable name, so the multiplication runs normally rather than being skipped, and embedding expressions in strings is precisely what template literals were created for - the syntax has been fully valid since ES2015, no error here. The string would only print ${...} literally if it were wrapped in single or double quotes instead of backticks - mixing up the quote type is the most common real-world template-literal mistake.

lessons.title: Comparisons === and the == trap
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 9: Comparisons === and the == trap

theory.contentHtml:
Data arriving from CSV files or APIs is rarely clean: numeric columns come in as strings, empty cells come in as empty strings. JavaScript has two ways to ask "are these two values equal", and the one that looks more familiar - two equals signs - happily answers true for "5" and 5. This lesson shows why three equals signs is the default, and where data types quietly wreck threshold checks too.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Triple equals: strict comparison
  2. Double equals: implicit coercion and its traps
  3. Greater than, less than
  4. Key points

1. Triple equals: strict comparison

=== returns true when two values have the same type and the same value - nothing more, nothing less. !== is its negation. Neither ever converts types for you:

const quantity = 5;

console.log(quantity === 5);    // true: same type, same value
console.log(quantity === "5");  // false: number vs string
console.log(quantity !== 10);   // true: different value

The second line is the one that pays off for data people. The number 5 and the string "5" print identically on screen, but their types differ - and data read from a CSV is all strings until you deliberately convert it. === returns false on the spot, so the bug surfaces early instead of silently corrupting a number at the end of the pipeline.

The correct move when data arrives as strings: convert explicitly, then compare:

const rawRevenue = "120";

console.log(rawRevenue === 120);          // false: still a string
console.log(Number(rawRevenue) === 120);  // true: convert first, then compare

2. Double equals: implicit coercion and its traps

== (and !=) does one extra thing before comparing: if the two sides have different types, it converts one or both sides following its own set of rules - this is implicit coercion. Those rules are convoluted enough to produce results like these:

console.log("5" == 5);           // true: the string is coerced to a number
console.log(0 == "");            // true: both sides end up as 0
console.log(0 == "0");           // true: "0" is coerced to 0
console.log("" == "0");          // false: two strings, no coercion, different content
console.log(null == undefined);  // true: a special case in the spec

Look closely at the middle three lines: 0 equals "", 0 equals "0", yet "" does not equal "0". An "equals" that is not transitive is not something you can trust to build logic on.

For data people, the most dangerous trap is that it erases the boundary between missing data and the value 0 - two entirely different business situations:

const rawQuantity = "";  // an empty cell read from a CSV file

console.log(rawQuantity == 0);   // true: the empty cell "passes" as zero
console.log(rawQuantity === 0);  // false: an empty cell is not the number 0

Filter for "orders with quantity 0" using == 0 and you will sweep in the blank rows as well - with no error thrown to make you suspicious.

The rule of this course, and of most serious codebases: always use === and !==. The coercion rules of == are not worth memorizing - knowing they exist is enough to read old code.

3. Greater than, less than

The four operators >, <, >=, <= handle threshold checks - everyday work when tiering, filtering, and alerting:

const revenue = 1500000;

console.log(revenue > 1000000);   // true
console.log(revenue >= 1500000);  // true: "greater or equal" includes equality
console.log(revenue < 500000);    // false

The boundary between > and >= is where business logic goes wrong most often: "orders of 1 million and up" is >= 1000000, while > 1000000 wrongly excludes an order of exactly 1 million. Read the requirement carefully before choosing.

And a trap from the same family as section 2: comparing two strings does not compare numeric values - it compares character by character in code order:

console.log(9 > 10);      // false: number comparison
console.log("9" > "10");  // true: string comparison goes character by character

"9" > "10" is true because the character "9" sorts after the character "1". Sort or threshold-check a numeric column that was never converted and this is exactly what you get - one more reason to Number(...) before comparing.

All three sections above compare two values against each other. The next lesson turns to a different question: when a single value stands where a condition belongs, does JavaScript read it as true or as false?

Key points

=== and !== are the default. Strict comparison never converts types for you - different types mean false immediately, so bugs surface early instead of silently corrupting numbers.

== coerces implicitly, following rules nobody remembers. "5" == 5, 0 == "", null == undefined are all true - it erases the boundary between missing data and the value 0. Know it to read old code; never write it.

String versus string compares character by character. "9" > "10" is true. Numeric columns read from CSV need Number(...) before any threshold check or sort.

lessons.title: Truthy and falsy the six values treated as empty
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 10: Truthy and falsy the six values treated as empty

theory.contentHtml:
A condition in JavaScript does not have to be true or false. Hand it a string, a number, a cell read from a file - JavaScript accepts it and converts that value to a boolean using one short list. The list holds exactly six entries, and one of them is the number 0 - which is where data people pay the price, because a stock level of 0 or a discount of 0 is real data, not an empty cell.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. The six falsy values
  2. The zero trap: falsy but real data
  3. Key points

1. The six falsy values

When a non-boolean value stands in a condition, JavaScript converts it to true or false. The Boolean(...) function lets you preview that conversion. The complete falsy list - values treated as false - has exactly 6 entries:

console.log(Boolean(false));      // false
console.log(Boolean(0));          // false
console.log(Boolean(""));         // false: empty string
console.log(Boolean(null));       // false
console.log(Boolean(undefined));  // false
console.log(Boolean(NaN));        // false

Six values, learnable in a minute, and that is the whole rule. Every other value is truthy - including a few that look very "empty":

console.log(Boolean("0"));       // true: a non-empty string, even if it spells zero
console.log(Boolean(" "));       // true: a space is still a character
console.log(Boolean("false"));   // true: the word false is just text
console.log(Boolean(-1));        // true: any non-zero number

The first three lines share one reason: each is a string with at least one character. Only the empty string "" is on the falsy list; JavaScript never reads what is inside a string to judge it. A CSV cell spelling "0", or a cell holding a single space, still counts as "something is there" - worth remembering when you clean data.

2. The zero trap: falsy but real data

Data people meet truthy/falsy most often in the "does this cell have data" check. Writing Boolean(cell) gets it done in one line, but that shortcut files the number 0 under the same heading as an empty cell:

const discount = 0;   // a real value: this order simply has no discount
const note = "";      // this cell was left empty in the source file

console.log(Boolean(discount));  // false: a real 0 gets reported as "missing"
console.log(Boolean(note));      // false: correct here, the cell really is empty

Both lines print false, yet only one of them is the right answer. A report that filters for "rows with missing data" this way will dump every zero-discount order and every zero-stock item into the error list.

The right way to ask is to compare explicitly against whatever the source uses to mark an empty cell. CSV files usually leave an empty string; APIs usually return null:

const discount = 0;
const note = "";
const shippedAt = null;

console.log(discount !== "");     // true: 0 is a real value, not an empty cell
console.log(note !== "");         // false: this cell is empty
console.log(shippedAt !== null);  // false: the API marks this field as missing

An explicit comparison costs a few extra characters and states exactly what you count as "missing" - so the next person reading the code does not have to guess. The next lesson, on if, will use this rule constantly.

Key points

There are exactly 6 falsy values: false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy.

The strings "0" and " " are truthy. Only the empty string is falsy; JavaScript does not read a string's contents to judge it.

0 is falsy yet usually valid data. Zero stock and zero discount are real numbers - the Boolean(cell) shortcut misreports them as missing.

Ask "is there data here" with an explicit comparison. Compare against the marker the source actually uses for an empty cell (!== "" for CSV, !== null for APIs) instead of leaning on truthiness.

lessons.title: Branching if, else if, else
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 12: Branching if, else if, else

theory.contentHtml:
Most business logic is labeling by threshold: orders of 5 million and up are VIP, stock below 10 triggers an alert, a score under 50 is a fail. if/else turns those thresholds into code - and the order you write the conditions in decides whether the labels come out right or wrong, with no error to tell you when they are wrong.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. if: run when the condition is true
  2. else and else if: tiering orders by value
  3. Condition order: high thresholds first
  4. The ternary operator for short cases
  5. Key points

1. if: run when the condition is true

if takes a condition in parentheses; when the condition is true (or truthy - the "Truthy and falsy" lesson), the block in curly braces runs, otherwise it is skipped entirely:

const orderAmount = 6200000;

if (orderAmount >= 5000000) {
  console.log("High-value order");
}

console.log("Done");

Two things worth noting:

  • The if block runs 0 or 1 times - there is no such thing as running halfway. Change orderAmount to 200000 and the "High-value order" line disappears, while "Done" still prints because it sits outside the block.
  • The curly braces { } define the block's extent. A braceless one-line if works, but add a second line and that line quietly stands outside the condition - a classic mistake. This course always writes the braces.

2. else and else if: tiering orders by value

Labeling usually has more than two outcomes. An if / else if / else chain handles a complete tiering rule:

const orderAmount = 1500000;

if (orderAmount >= 5000000) {
  console.log("VIP");
} else if (orderAmount >= 1000000) {
  console.log("Standard");
} else {
  console.log("Small");
}

How this chain executes matters more than its syntax:

  • Conditions are tried top to bottom; the first true one runs its branch and then the whole chain exits - conditions below it are never tried.
  • That is why the else if (orderAmount >= 1000000) branch effectively means "from 1 million up to below 5 million" - the "below 5 million" part needs no writing, because anyone reaching this line has already failed the condition above.
  • The final else is the safety net: every case that matched no condition. With an else, exactly one branch always runs; without one, it is possible that no branch runs.

3. Condition order: high thresholds first

Swap the first two conditions of the example above and you have a bug that will never raise an error:

const orderAmount = 6200000;

// WRONG - the low threshold is checked first and catches everything
if (orderAmount >= 1000000) {
  console.log("Standard");
} else if (orderAmount >= 5000000) {
  console.log("VIP");  // unreachable: any amount >= 5000000 is also >= 1000000
} else {
  console.log("Small");
}

A 6,200,000 order entering this chain gets labeled "Standard": it satisfies the first condition >= 1000000 right away, the chain exits, and the >= 5000000 condition is never asked. The VIP branch becomes dead code - every order is either Standard or Small, the tier report is wrong for the entire top segment, and the program runs on as if nothing happened.

The rule to take away: overlapping thresholds go from high to low (or from strict to loose). An order only gets considered for a lower tier after failing the higher one - exactly how tiering works in real life.

4. The ternary operator for short cases

When the branch is merely "pick one of two values", the ternary operator beats a four-line if/else block. Its skeleton:

condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse

In real use:

const revenue = 8500000;
const label = revenue >= 5000000 ? "high" : "normal";

console.log(label);  // high

The key difference from if: a ternary is an expression - it produces a value, so it can be assigned straight into a variable as above. if is a statement and cannot.

Its limits are equally clear: exactly two outcomes, choosing a value. Three or more thresholds, or branches that need several statements, call for if / else if - nested ternaries are exhausting to read, and the next reader is usually you.

Key points

An if/else if chain tries top to bottom and exits at the first match. Every else if carries the implicit condition "already failed everything above" - use that so you never restate the upper bound.

Overlapping thresholds must go from high to low. Put the low threshold first and the high branch becomes dead code: labels wrong across the board, not a single error line. This is the most expensive kind of bug in data work - numbers still come out, they just come out wrong.

else is the safety net. With it, exactly one branch always runs; without it, you accept that some cases run no branch - make that a deliberate choice.

Ternaries are for two-way value picks only. From three thresholds up, return to if/else if so the next person can still read it.

lessons.title: Loops for, while, break and continue
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 14: Loops for, while, break and continue

theory.contentHtml:
A file of 10,000 orders cannot be processed with 10,000 lines of code. Loops let you write the logic once and apply it to every row of data - accumulating revenue, counting valid rows, scanning for outliers. This lesson covers three loop forms and the two keywords that control which iterations count.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. The classic for loop
  2. for...of: iterating straight over an array
  3. while: looping without a known count
  4. break and continue
  5. The infinite loop trap
  6. Key points

1. The classic for loop

The counting loop with an i variable - three parts separated by semicolons: initialization; continue-condition; step:

for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
  console.log("Processing row", i);
}

Run it and watch i go from 0 to 4 - the condition i < 5 is checked before each iteration, so the i = 5 iteration never happens. Counting from 0 is a habit worth keeping: array indexes start at 0 too, as you will see later. The counter is declared with let because i++ reassigns it every iteration.

The most-used loop pattern in data work is accumulation - declare a total outside the loop, add to it each iteration:

let total = 0;

for (let i = 1; i <= 12; i++) {
  total = total + i;
}

console.log(total);  // 78: the sum 1 + 2 + ... + 12

Every "total revenue" and "order count" you compute later is a variation of this pattern.

2. for...of: iterating straight over an array

Real data lives in arrays - lists of values in square brackets. Arrays get their own module (module 4), but you can already traverse one today: for...of hands you each element directly, no index required:

const revenues = [1200000, 800000, 2500000];

let total = 0;
for (const revenue of revenues) {
  total = total + revenue;
}

console.log(total);  // 4500000

Read it as: "for each revenue of revenues". Compared with the classic for, there is no i and no stop-condition to write yourself - the loop ends when the array does, so there is no room left for an off-by-one mistake. The loop variable can be declared with const because each iteration gets a fresh binding; nothing is reassigned.

Which form to choose: you need the element itself → for...of; you need the index (printing row numbers, comparing neighbors) or a step other than 1 → the classic for.

3. while: looping without a known count

while has only a condition - while it holds, the loop keeps going. It fits problems shaped like "loop until" rather than "loop N times":

let stock = 50;   // units in the warehouse
let orders = 0;   // wholesale orders we can accept, 12 units each

while (stock >= 12) {
  stock = stock - 12;
  orders = orders + 1;
}

console.log(orders);  // 4
console.log(stock);   // 2: not enough left for a fifth order

Nobody counted the iterations up front - the condition decides. Change the starting stock to 11 and the body never runs at all: while checks its condition before the first iteration.

4. break and continue

Two keywords that steer a loop from the inside:

  • continue - skip the rest of this iteration, move on to the next.
  • break - exit the loop entirely, no further iterations.

continue is the data person's most familiar tool: scanning a list while skipping missing values. Missing data in JavaScript is usually marked with null:

const amounts = [1200000, null, 2500000, null, 800000];

let total = 0;
for (const amount of amounts) {
  if (amount === null) {
    continue;  // skip missing values
  }
  total = total + amount;
}

console.log(total);  // 4500000: only the three real values are summed

Without the continue line, total + null would still run (JavaScript quietly treats null as 0 in numeric addition) - the total happens to survive, but the logic is wrong: counting rows or averaging would expose it immediately. Filtering explicitly with === null and continue states the intent: missing values take no part in the calculation.

break fits "found it, done" problems:

const amounts = [1200000, 800000, 5200000, 900000];

for (const amount of amounts) {
  if (amount >= 5000000) {
    console.log("Found a big order:", amount);
    break;  // stop scanning, no need to look further
  }
}

In a million-row list where the target sits on row three, break saves the remaining 999,997 iterations.

5. The infinite loop trap

A while loop whose condition never changes never stops:

// WRONG - stock is never updated, the condition stays true forever
let stock = 50;

while (stock >= 12) {
  console.log("Take one order");
}

Compare with the example in section 3: the one missing line is stock = stock - 12. The condition stock >= 12 stays true forever, the loop runs forever, the tab freezes. With while, updating the variables in the condition is entirely your responsibility - the classic for is less prone to this because the i++ step is built into the syntax, but write the step backwards (i-- against a i < n condition) and you are just as stuck.

Before running any while loop, ask one question: "Which variable in the condition changes, and on which line?" If you cannot point at it, do not run the loop.

Key points

Classic for: initialization; condition; step. The condition is checked before each iteration. The accumulation pattern - total outside the loop, built up inside - is the foundation of every sum and count to come.

for...of hands you elements directly and stops when the array ends. Need the element itself, use it; need the index or a custom step, return to the classic for. Arrays get full coverage in module 4 - traversing them is enough for today.

continue skips the iteration, break abandons the loop. Scanning data while skipping null is continue's job; found-it-stop-looking is break's.

while updates nothing on its own. An unchanging condition is an infinite loop. Point at the line that moves the condition toward false before you run it.

questions.prompt: Which of these expressions returns false?

options.label: C
options.text: null == undefined

questions.explanation: Only "5" === 5 returns false: triple equals compares strictly - both sides must have the same type and the same value - and the string "5" and the number 5 differ in type, so it is false immediately, with no conversion step. The other three expressions all use == - the implicitly coercing comparison - so they all return true: "5" == 5 converts the string to a number before comparing, 0 == "" brings both sides to 0 (the very trap that erases the boundary between an empty cell and a quantity of 0), and null == undefined is a special case the spec defines in advance. Those three true results are also why the course rule is to always use ===/!==: a type mismatch shows up immediately as false, surfacing the bug early instead of silently corrupting numbers at the end of the pipeline.

questions.prompt: Which of these values is truthy?

options.label: B
options.text: "" (the empty string)

options.label: C
options.text: "0" (a string containing the character 0)

options.label: D
options.text: undefined

questions.explanation: The falsy list has exactly 6 entries: false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN - every other value is truthy. "0" is not on that list: it is a non-empty string (one character long), so Boolean("0") is true. Do not confuse it with the number 0 - the number 0 sits squarely among the 6 falsy values, and it is the trap most worth remembering for data people: a discount of 0 or a stock level of 0 is valid data, yet a truthiness check treats it as "missing", which is why the "has data" question must compare explicitly against whatever marker the source uses for an empty cell. The empty string "" is falsy too - quite unlike the one-character string "0", and that very difference is why 0 == "" and 0 == "0" are both true while "" == "0" is false. As for undefined, it is falsy as well, in the same group as null.

options.label: A
options.text: VIP

options.label: B
options.text: Standard

options.label: C
options.text: Small

options.label: D
options.text: Both Standard and VIP

questions.explanation: An if/else if chain tries its conditions top to bottom and exits at the first true one. 7000000 >= 1000000 is true, so the first branch runs, prints Standard, and the whole chain ends - the >= 5000000 condition is never asked. Although 7 million is indeed VIP by the business rule, the VIP branch here has become dead code: any value satisfying >= 5000000 has already satisfied >= 1000000 first. Small cannot happen either, since else only runs when every condition above it has failed. And nothing ever prints both labels: an if/else if chain runs exactly one branch - unlike a series of separate if statements, whose conditions are tested independently. This is the classic "low threshold first" bug: the program reports no error and quietly mislabels the entire top segment - the fix is to order overlapping thresholds from high to low.

questions.prompt: When is the classic for loop (counting with i) the better choice over for...of?

options.label: A
options.text: When you need the element's index, or a step other than 1

options.label: B
options.text: When traversing sequentially from the first element to the last

options.label: C
options.text: When the array is large, because the classic for runs much faster

options.label: D
options.text: for...of only works on arrays of numbers, so arrays of strings require the classic for

questions.explanation: The classic for keeps the one thing for...of deliberately hides: the counter. Printing row numbers, comparing an element with its neighbor (i versus i - 1), or stepping through every second element - that is classic-for territory. Plain sequential traversal is the opposite case: that is exactly what for...of is for - no stop-condition to write, the loop ends when the array does, leaving no room for off-by-one mistakes. Nor is the speed difference between the two forms a basis for choosing at this level - the thing worth optimizing is readability, and whichever loop states the intent more clearly wins. As for the idea that for...of only accepts arrays of numbers, that is simply not true: it traverses arrays holding any value type - numbers, strings, or a mix - it does not care what the elements are.

questions.prompt: Inside a loop, how do break and continue differ?

options.label: A
options.text: break skips the current iteration; continue exits the loop entirely

options.label: B
options.text: break exits the loop entirely; continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next

options.label: C
options.text: They do the same thing; break is the older spelling of continue

options.label: D
options.text: continue only works inside while, and break only inside for

questions.explanation: break ends the loop on the spot - no further iterations, execution resumes after the loop; it fits "found it, done" problems: scanning a million rows where the target sits on row three means the rest need never be checked. continue is gentler: it only skips the rest of the current iteration, and the loop then carries on with the next element - exactly the scan-while-skipping-missing-values pattern (amount === null triggers continue, and the real rows still get summed in full). The option stating the reverse sounds very close to the right answer but has the two keyword names swapped - read carefully before picking. Nor are the two keywords one and the same: mistake one for the other and the loop either stops too early or runs too much. And both work in every loop form - for, for...of, and while all accept both break and continue; neither keyword is tied to one particular kind of loop.

options.label: D
options.text: An error, because null cannot be added

questions.explanation: The loop visits all 4 elements, but on the two iterations that meet null, the condition amount === null is true and continue runs - the rest of that iteration (the count = count + 1 line) is skipped and the loop moves to the next element. Only the two iterations meeting 500000 and 2000000 reach the counting line, so count ends at 2. The number 4 is the count of iterations, not of how many times the counting line ran - continue does not stop the loop, but it does block the body below it. Nor can count end at 0: continue skips only the null iterations, and the two real values still get counted - mistaking continue for break is what produces the closest wrong scenario, stopping at the second element with count left at 1. And no error occurs: this code never adds amount to anything - it only counts - and even if it did, JavaScript throws no error on null in numeric addition (it quietly treats null as 0, one more reason to filter missing values explicitly, as this code does).

lessons.title: Functions packaging a computation
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 17: Functions packaging a computation

theory.contentHtml:
A revenue analysis script repeats a handful of familiar computations: converting VND to millions, computing percentages, rounding. Copy the formula everywhere and the day the team changes the rounding convention, you have to fix every copy and hope you missed none. Functions exist to gather a computation into exactly one place.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Declaring and calling a function
  2. Parameters: the inputs of a function
  3. Default parameters
  4. Key points

1. Declaring and calling a function

Three orders, the same conversion to millions of VND, copied three times:

console.log(45600000 / 1000000);
console.log(1250000 / 1000000);
console.log(8900000 / 1000000);

Output:

45.6
1.25
8.9

Tomorrow the team agrees on a new convention - "reports keep 1 decimal digit only" - and you have to find all three places, thirty places in a real script, and fix each one. Miss one and the report carries two inconsistent number formats.

Package the computation into a function and the formula lives in a single place:

function toMillions(amountVnd) {
  return amountVnd / 1000000;
}

console.log(toMillions(45600000));
console.log(toMillions(1250000));
console.log(toMillions(8900000));

Output:

45.6
1.25
8.9

Read the declaration piece by piece:

  • function - the keyword that opens a function declaration.
  • toMillions - the function's name, taken from a verb or from the meaning of its result, in English like any variable name.
  • (amountVnd) - a parameter: a variable standing in for the input, which exists only inside the function.
  • The curly braces { } wrap the function body.
  • return - the value the function hands back to whoever called it.

Declaring a function does not run it. It only runs when it is called: write its name followed by parentheses holding the input - toMillions(45600000). That whole call expression becomes the returned value, which is why wrapping it in console.log(...) prints the result.

2. Parameters: the inputs of a function

A function can take several parameters, separated by commas. The average value of an order needs both revenue and order count:

function revenuePerOrder(revenue, orders) {
  return revenue / orders;
}

console.log(revenuePerOrder(45600000, 128));

Output:

356250

Two easily-confused words, settled once and for all: a parameter is the name in the declaration - revenue, orders; an argument is the actual value at the call site - 45600000, 128.

Arguments match parameters by position: the first value goes into revenue, the second into orders. Calling revenuePerOrder(128, 45600000) still runs - it just produces a meaningless number. JavaScript does not guess your intent.

And what if a call passes too few arguments? The missing parameter gets undefined, and dividing by undefined yields NaN:

function revenuePerOrder(revenue, orders) {
  return revenue / orders;
}

console.log(revenuePerOrder(45600000));

Output:

NaN

No error is thrown - just a silent garbage value flowing on into every later computation. When NaN shows up in your output, the first suspect to check is a function call missing an argument.

3. Default parameters

Some parameters receive the same value almost every time. Instead of forcing every call to repeat it, declare a default value right in the parameter list with =:

function formatRevenue(amount, unit = "million VND") {
  return (amount / 1000000).toFixed(1) + " " + unit;
}

console.log(formatRevenue(45600000));
console.log(formatRevenue(45600000, "M"));

Output:

45.6 million VND
45.6 M

(toFixed(1) rounds to 1 decimal digit - and note: it returns a string, not a number.)

Call without unit → "million VND" is used. Pass "M" → the passed value wins. The default only applies when the argument is left out (or is undefined) - 0 and the empty string "" are real values and do not trigger the default. Good habit: put parameters with defaults at the end of the list, so calls can omit the tail without breaking the order of the head.

Key points

A function is a named computation: declare once, call many times. When the formula changes, you fix exactly one place - that is the reason functions exist.

Declaring a function does not run it. It runs only when a call functionName(...) appears, and that call carries the returned value back to where it stands.

Arguments match parameters by position; missing ones become undefined. Computing with undefined yields NaN without any error to warn you.

A default parameter only kicks in when the argument is left out or is undefined - 0 and "" are real values and never fall back to the default.

lessons.title: return handing a value back to the code
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 18: return handing a value back to the code

theory.contentHtml:
Every function in the previous lesson ended with return. Beginners often replace it with console.log: a test run shows the expected number on screen, so they move on - and then the next computation produces NaN with no error line pointing anywhere. This lesson separates the two statements.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. return vs console.log
  2. return ends the function immediately
  3. Key points

1. return vs console.log

The two statements do completely different jobs:

  • console.log - puts text on the screen for a human to read. Once printed, the code keeps nothing.
  • return - hands a value back to the code to be used further: assigned to a variable, computed with, passed to another function.

The familiar wrong version - a function that "prints the result" instead of returning it:

// Wrong - prints the result instead of returning it
function toMillions(amountVnd) {
  console.log(amountVnd / 1000000);
}

const inMillions = toMillions(45600000);
console.log(inMillions + 10);

Output:

45.6
NaN

The printed 45.6 makes the function look correct - that is exactly the trap. But the function has no return, so it returns undefined; inMillions receives undefined, and undefined + 10 is NaN. The result flashed on the screen and vanished - the code never got to touch it.

The correct version:

function toMillions(amountVnd) {
  return amountVnd / 1000000;
}

const inMillions = toMillions(45600000);
console.log(inMillions + 10);

Output:

55.6

The rule of thumb: if the result needs to be used further → return. If you only want to look at a value while testing → console.log outside the function, wrapped around the call.

2. return ends the function immediately

return does not only hand a value over, it also ends the function on the spot - no line after it runs. That property makes classification functions very compact:

function classifyOrder(amount) {
  if (amount >= 10000000) {
    return "large";
  }
  return "normal";
}

console.log(classifyOrder(45600000));
console.log(classifyOrder(1250000));

Output:

large
normal

With 45600000, the function enters the if branch, returns "large" and stops - the return "normal" line never runs on that call. With 1250000, the condition is false, the function slides past the if block and returns "normal". No else is needed here: once the branch above exits for good, the rest of the body is the other branch by definition.

The opposite case is worth remembering too: a function that runs through its whole body without meeting any return hands back undefined - exactly what happened in section 1.

Key points

return hands a value back to the code; console.log only puts text on the screen. A function that prints its result without return returns undefined - the output looks right, but every computation using it yields NaN. This is the number-one beginner mistake with functions.

return ends the function immediately. No line after an executed return runs on that call - which is why multi-branch functions need no else.

A function that meets no return hands back undefined. No error, no warning - just an empty value flowing on downstream.

lessons.title: Arrow functions the shorthand you'll meet everywhere
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 20: Arrow functions the shorthand you'll meet everywhere

theory.contentHtml:
The two theory lessons so far wrote functions with function. Open any JavaScript codebase written after 2015 and you will meet a second notation everywhere: the arrow =>. Skip it and reading other people's code feels like missing half the alphabet - and from the array module onward, you will be writing it daily yourself.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. One function, two ways to write it
  2. Implicit return: drop the braces, drop the return
  3. When you still need braces
  4. Arrow functions as callbacks
  5. Which style to choose
  6. Key points

1. One function, two ways to write it

The to-millions conversion from the first lesson of this module, written both ways:

function toMillionsDecl(amountVnd) {
  return amountVnd / 1000000;
}

const toMillionsArrow = (amountVnd) => {
  return amountVnd / 1000000;
};

console.log(toMillionsDecl(45600000));
console.log(toMillionsArrow(45600000));

Output:

45.6
45.6

Read the arrow declaration piece by piece: (amountVnd) is the parameter list, => replaces the function keyword, and what follows the arrow is the body. The whole thing is a value - a nameless function - assigned to const toMillionsArrow, exactly the way you assign a number or a string to a variable. Calling it is no different: name + parentheses + arguments.

Written with full braces like this, the arrow is barely shorter. The real power is in the next section.

2. Implicit return: drop the braces, drop the return

When the body is a single expression, an arrow function lets you drop both the braces and the return keyword - the expression after the arrow automatically becomes the return value. This is called an implicit return:

const toMillions = (amountVnd) => amountVnd / 1000000;
const discountedPrice = (price) => price * 0.75;

console.log(toMillions(45600000));
console.log(discountedPrice(500000));

Output:

45.6
375000

Each function fits on one line and still returns a proper value - toMillions(45600000) can be used in any further computation as usual.

The trap is mixing the two styles: adding braces switches implicit return off. Braces tell JavaScript "this is a multi-statement body", and a body needs an explicit return:

// Wrong - braces start a function body, so this returns undefined
const discountedPrice = (price) => { price * 0.75 };

console.log(discountedPrice(500000));

This function runs without any error: the multiplication is computed… and thrown away, and the function returns undefined. The same silent-failure family as a function that forgets its return in the previous lesson - everything looks fine until a garbage number surfaces at the end of the pipeline.

One small detail: a function with exactly one parameter may drop the parentheses around it (amount => amount / 2). This course keeps the parentheses in every example for consistency - both forms are correct.

3. When you still need braces

When the body has more than one statement - say it contains an if - you must go back to braces plus an explicit return, even in an arrow function:

const shippingFee = (total) => {
  if (total >= 500000) {
    return 0;
  }
  return 30000;
};

console.log(shippingFee(600000));
console.log(shippingFee(200000));

Output:

0
30000

Orders from 500 thousand VND ship free, the rest pay a 30-thousand fee - two-branch logic has no business being squeezed into a single expression. The rule is mechanical: one expression → braces may go; multiple statements → braces + return.

4. Arrow functions as callbacks

The reason arrows are everywhere is not that they save a few characters at declaration - it is that in JavaScript, a function is a value you can pass to another function. A function passed along like that is called a callback, and arrow syntax exists to write callbacks that fit on one line.

A first taste of the next module - map applies a function to every element of an array:

const revenues = [1200000, 4500000, 800000];
const inMillions = revenues.map((amount) => amount / 1000000);

console.log(inMillions);

Output:

[
  1.2,
  4.5,
  0.8
]

Look closely at the argument to map: (amount) => amount / 1000000 - a complete function, declared right where it is used, no name needed. Writing it with function works too, but is visibly clunkier. The entire next module (map, filter, reduce) is chains of exactly this - this lesson is the paving for that road.

How map works is next module's business; the only thing to carry away today is the shape of the syntax: an arrow function sitting inside another function's call.

5. Which style to choose

Both notations define functions; the remaining differences are where they fit and one background behavior:

  • Function declarations for the "main" functions of a script - named functions called from several places. Declarations are also hoisted: JavaScript lifts them up front, so a call on a line above the declaration still works. A function assigned to a const is not - declare first, call after.
  • Arrow functions for callbacks and one-liners assigned to variables - exactly where they shine.

There is one more difference between the two: how they treat the keyword this. That concept is outside the scope of this course - working with plain data, numbers, strings and arrays, you will not need it.

Key points

An arrow function is a function written with =>, assigned to a variable as a value. Calling it works exactly like a regular function; the differences are syntax and where it fits.

A single expression → implicit return. (x) => x * 2 returns its result automatically. But adding braces switches implicit return off - (x) => { x * 2 } returns undefined, runs without error, and fails silently.

Multiple statements need braces plus an explicit return - even inside an arrow function.

Arrows shine in the callback position - a function passed to another function, declared right at the point of use. The upcoming map/filter/reduce module stands on this foundation.

The this difference between arrows and regular functions is out of scope - no need to care while working with plain data.

lessons.title: Scope where variables live and die
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 22: Scope where variables live and die

theory.contentHtml:
So far in this module, variables have simply been declared and used. But try to console.log a parameter outside its function and you get an instant ReferenceError - variables in JavaScript have a clearly bounded living area. This lesson shows where that area is, so that next time you read an "is not defined" error you know exactly what to look for.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. What scope is
  2. Block scope of let and const
  3. Variables inside a function stay inside
  4. Key points

1. What scope is

The scope of a variable is the region of code where that variable exists and can be referred to by name. Outside that region, the name might as well never have been declared. For let and const, the rule fits in one sentence: a variable lives inside the nearest pair of curly braces { } enclosing it - when the braces close, the variable's life ends.

That pair of braces can be the body of an if block, a loop body, or a function body. A variable declared outside every brace lives for the whole file - a global variable of the script.

2. Block scope of let and const

Watch the rule in action inside an if block:

const total = 620000;

if (total > 500000) {
  const label = "large order";
  console.log(label);
}

console.log(total);

Output:

large order
620000

label is declared inside the if block, so it is usable there; total is declared outside, so it is usable in both places. The reverse direction does not work:

if (total > 500000) {
  const label = "large order";
}

console.log(label); // ReferenceError: label is not defined

Once the if block closes, label is gone. Note the error carefully: ReferenceError - the name does not exist - which is different from undefined - the name exists but holds no value yet. Need the block's result outside? Declare the variable with let before the block and assign inside it - exactly the pattern from the conditionals lesson.

3. Variables inside a function stay inside

A function body is also a pair of curly braces, so every variable declared inside a function - parameters included - lives only inside it:

function averageOrder(revenue, orders) {
  const average = revenue / orders;
  return average;
}

console.log(averageOrder(45600000, 128));

Output:

356250

Whereas reading average or revenue from outside the function:

console.log(average); // ReferenceError: average is not defined
console.log(revenue); // ReferenceError: revenue is not defined

This is a feature, not a limitation. A function is a closed room: the outside world sees exactly two things - arguments going in and the return value coming out. Every intermediate variable (average, counters, temporaries) is internal business that cannot collide with the rest of the script. That is why two different functions can both name a variable total without stepping on each other - precious once an analysis script grows to a few hundred lines.

To get a result out, the road worth taking is return - receive it and assign it to a variable outside. The door of this room is not actually locked, though, and what happens when a function reaches through it is the next lesson.

Key points

A let/const variable lives inside its nearest pair of curly braces. When the if block or function body ends, the variable is gone.

ReferenceError is not undefined. The first means the name does not exist, the second means the name exists but holds no value - two situations with different fixes.

Variables inside a function - parameters included - are the function's internal business. The outside sees only arguments going in and the return value coming out. That is the feature that keeps functions from stepping on each other.

To use a block's result outside the block, declare the variable before the block and assign inside - for a function, the way out is return.

lessons.title: When a function reaches outside itself
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 23: When a function reaches outside itself

theory.contentHtml:
The previous lesson concluded that a function is a closed room: the outside sees only arguments going in and the return value coming out. But JavaScript does not lock that door - code inside a function can still read, and still modify, variables declared outside it. Two things commonly happen when the door opens: names collide, and functions modify outer variables directly.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Shadowing: same name, two different variables
  2. Side effects: changing outer variables from inside a function
  3. Key points

1. Shadowing: same name, two different variables

What happens when a variable inside a function has the same name as one outside?

const rate = 0.5;

function discountedPrice(price) {
  const rate = 0.25;
  return price * (1 - rate);
}

console.log(discountedPrice(400000));
console.log(rate);

Output:

300000
0.5

The two rate variables are entirely different variables. Inside the function, the local rate (0.25) hides the outer one - this is called shadowing - so the computation uses 0.25 and yields 300000. Outside the function, the outer rate is still intact at 0.5: it was never touched, only temporarily hidden by name.

JavaScript's lookup rule: on meeting a name, search the nearest scope first, and only widen outward when nothing is found. Shadowing is not a syntax error, but it is a chronic source of misreading - the reader assumes the outer variable is in play while the function uses the inner one. Avoid it when you can: more specific names (discountRate, vatRate) end the problem.

2. Side effects: changing outer variables from inside a function

Unlike reading, JavaScript does not forbid a function from assigning a new value to a let variable declared outside it:

let totalRevenue = 0;

function addOrder(amount) {
  totalRevenue = totalRevenue + amount;
}

addOrder(250000);
addOrder(180000);
console.log(totalRevenue);

Output:

430000

It runs correctly - and that is precisely what makes it dangerous. A function reaching out to modify the world around it is called a side effect, and it makes code fragile in several ways:

  • The result depends on call history. addOrder(250000) run once gives 250000; accidentally run twice gives 500000 - same line of code, two results. The function can no longer be predicted from its arguments.
  • Understanding the function means reading the whole script. Where is totalRevenue declared, and who else is modifying it? The closed room from the previous lesson is now wide open.
  • It is hard to test. Trying the function on different data means remembering to reset totalRevenue = 0 before every run - forget once and the result is silently wrong.

Compare with the clean function version - every input through parameters, every output through return:

function sumOrders(orderA, orderB) {
  return orderA + orderB;
}

const totalRevenue = sumOrders(250000, 180000);
console.log(totalRevenue);

Output:

430000

Same answer, but sumOrders gives it no matter how many times, where, or in what order it is called - because it touches nothing outside its own scope. The principle to carry through the rest of the course: a function takes parameters and returns a result; it does not reach out and modify outer variables. In the next module, the functions you pass to map/filter must be clean in exactly this way for the results to be predictable.

Key points

A reused name is shadowing: two different variables, the inner hiding the outer. Not an error, but easy to misread - use more specific names to sidestep it.

A function modifying outer variables is a side effect - it runs, but it is fragile. Results depend on call history, and the code is harder to understand and to test.

A clean function takes parameters and returns. Same arguments, same result, however many times you call it - the principle for the rest of the course.

questions.explanation: This is the return vs console.log trap. When double(5) is called, the console.log(n * 2) inside the function runs first and prints 10. But the function has no `return`, so its return value is undefined - result receives undefined, and console.log(result) prints undefined as the second line. For result to hold 10, the function would need return n * 2; a console.log inside the function does not turn what it prints into a return value. The order cannot flip either: the call double(5) must finish before the assignment completes, so 10 always appears first. And the last line raises no error - result was properly declared, it just holds undefined; printing a variable that holds undefined is very different from reading a name that was never declared, which is when you would get a ReferenceError.

questions.prompt: A function is declared as function formatAmount(amount, unit = "VND"). When is the default value "VND" used?

options.label: A
options.text: When the call passes no argument for unit, or passes exactly undefined

options.label: B
options.text: On every call - whatever is passed for unit is always ignored

options.label: C
options.text: When the argument passed is the empty string "" or the number 0

options.label: D
options.text: Only when the call passes no arguments at all, including amount

questions.explanation: A default parameter is a fallback: it is used only when the argument at that position is left out or is undefined. Calling formatAmount(500000) gives unit nothing, so it takes "VND"; calling formatAmount(120, "USD") passes a value, and the passed value wins - the default stays out of it. The most commonly confused point is the empty string and the number 0: they are real values, different from undefined, so the function uses them as-is and never falls back to the default. Nor is there any rule that all arguments must be missing: each parameter is considered independently - formatAmount(500000) still gets a perfectly good amount = 500000, and only unit is missing, so only unit takes its default.

options.label: D
options.text: The string "w * h"

questions.explanation: The curly braces after the arrow tell JavaScript this is a multi-statement function body - and a body needs an explicit return. Here w * h is computed to 6 and then thrown away; the function ends without returning anything, so it returns undefined. Notably, there is no error anywhere: braces are perfectly legal in an arrow function, they merely change the meaning from "one implicitly returned expression" to "a regular body" - the code runs quietly, fails without any warning, and that is exactly what makes it dangerous. To get 6, either drop the braces so the implicit return applies - (w, h) => w * h - or keep the braces and write the full { return w * h; }. As for the string "w * h", it cannot appear: w * h is an executed expression, not a string of characters - there are no quotes anywhere.
