questions.explanation: return ends the function immediately - code in a function does not run top to bottom regardless, it exits at the first return it reaches. For shippingFee(600000): the condition 600000 >= 500000 is true, the function executes return 0 and stops right there - the return 30000 line sits at the bottom but is never reached on this call, so it prints 0. For shippingFee(200000): the condition is false since 200000 < 500000, the if block is skipped, and the function falls through to return 30000, so it prints 30000. There is no path to undefined either: every way through this function ends at a return with a value - getting undefined would require running off the end of the function without hitting any return, which cannot happen here.

lessons.title: Arrays lists of values
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 26: Arrays lists of values

theory.contentHtml:
A revenue column in a spreadsheet, the list of orders an API returns, a sequence of sales region names - in JavaScript, they all live in an array. This lesson lays the groundwork: creating arrays, reading elements by position, counting them, and walking through every element. Adding, removing and slicing wait for the next lesson.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Creating arrays and zero-based indexes
  2. length: how long is the array
  3. Walking an array with for...of
  4. Key points

1. Creating arrays and zero-based indexes

An array is written with square brackets, values separated by commas. For data people, the most natural mental model: an array is one column of data - say, four days of revenue:

const revenues = [1200000, 950000, 1830000, 700000];
console.log(revenues[0]);
console.log(revenues[3]);
console.log(revenues[4]);
1200000
700000
undefined

Read one element with array_name[index], and etch this in right away: indexes start at 0. revenues[0] is the first element; revenues[3] is the fourth - which is also the last element of a 4-element array.

The third line deserves more attention: revenues[4] reaches past the end of the array, and JavaScript does not raise an error - it quietly returns undefined. Unlike many languages that stop the program on out-of-range access, here the undefined drifts on into the calculations below and produces a confusing result somewhere far away. When you see undefined in a result, suspect an index first.

Arrays hold values of any type - numbers, strings, booleans, and (from the "Objects: records with named fields" lesson on) records too:

const regions = ["North", "South", "Central"];
const flags = [true, false, true];
console.log(regions[1]);
console.log(flags[0]);
South
true

2. length: how long is the array

length tells you the number of elements. It is a property, not a function - no parentheses after it:

const regions = ["North", "South", "Central", "West"];
console.log(regions.length);
console.log(regions[regions.length - 1]);
4
West

The second line is an idiom you will meet daily: because indexes start at 0, the last element sits at position length - 1. A 4-element array → indexes run from 0 to 3. Writing regions[regions.length] asks for the fifth position of a 4-element array - and as in section 1, you get undefined, not an error.

3. Walking an array with for...of

To work with each element in turn, use for...of - on every pass, the variable declared after for receives one element, in order:

const orderAmounts = [250000, 1200000, 480000];
let total = 0;
for (const amount of orderAmounts) {
  total = total + amount;
}
console.log(total);
1930000

The pattern above - an accumulating variable initialized first, added to inside the loop, read afterwards - is how you total a column "by hand". It runs correctly and reads easily; a few lessons from now you meet more specialized tools (map, filter, reduce) for exactly this class of work, but for...of remains a trustworthy fallback whenever the logic gets complicated.

A loop is also the cheapest way to look at your data before processing it - print each element and check it is what you think it is:

const regions = ["North", "South", "Central"];
for (const region of regions) {
  console.log(region);
}
North
South
Central

Key points

Indexes start at 0; the last element sits at length - 1. This is the classic source of off-by-one errors - a 4-element array has no [4].

Out-of-range access returns undefined, with no error. An undefined slipping into a calculation causes a wrong result somewhere else - when you see one, check your indexes first.

length is a property, not a function. Writing regions.length() calls something that is not a function - and that one JavaScript really does throw on.

When you need each element, reach for for...of. No stop condition to write, the loop ends when the array does - no room left for off-by-one mistakes.

lessons.title: Working with arrays add, find, slice
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 27: Working with arrays add, find, slice

theory.contentHtml:
The previous lesson only read arrays. Real working lists move, though: a queue takes in new orders, a catalog has to be checked for a value, a report only wants the last few days. The three groups of methods below do those three jobs - plus the most important boundary: which ones modify the original array, and which ones return a new array.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Adding and removing at the end: push, pop
  2. Checking and locating: includes, indexOf
  3. Taking a section with slice
  4. Key points

1. Adding and removing at the end: push, pop

push adds an element to the end of the array; pop removes the last element and returns it:

const pendingOrders = ["ORD-101", "ORD-102"];
pendingOrders.push("ORD-103");
console.log(pendingOrders);

const lastOrder = pendingOrders.pop();
console.log(lastOrder);
console.log(pendingOrders);
[
  "ORD-101",
  "ORD-102",
  "ORD-103"
]
ORD-103
[
  "ORD-101",
  "ORD-102"
]

Two things to note:

  • push and pop modify the original array in place - after the call, the array is no longer what it was. Very different from slice in section 3 and the tools of the next few lessons, which always return a new array.
  • An array declared with const can still be push-ed. const only forbids reassigning the variable (pendingOrders = [...] is the error), not changing the array's contents.

The most common usage pattern: start with an empty array [] and push results into it inside a loop. Combine it with if and you have a manual filter:

const dailyRevenue = [500000, 1250000, 610000, 1830000];
const bigDays = [];
for (const revenue of dailyRevenue) {
  if (revenue >= 1000000) {
    bigDays.push(revenue);
  }
}
console.log(bigDays);
[
  1250000,
  1830000
]

Remember this rhythm - empty array, loop, push - because the next two lessons wrap it into a single method.

2. Checking and locating: includes, indexOf

Two questions that come up constantly when holding a list: "is this value in the list?" and "where is it?":

const categories = ["Electronics", "Furniture", "Toys"];
console.log(categories.includes("Furniture"));
console.log(categories.includes("Food"));
console.log(categories.indexOf("Toys"));
console.log(categories.indexOf("Food"));
true
false
2
-1
  • includes(value) returns true/false - perfect to drop straight into an if condition.
  • indexOf(value) returns the index of the first occurrence; when nothing is found it returns -1 (not undefined, and not an error). Testing "not present" with indexOf therefore means comparing against -1 - but if all you need is a yes/no, includes states the intent more directly.

Both comparisons are case-sensitive: categories.includes("furniture") is false. Real data dies at exactly this spot all the time - "North" in one file, "north" in another.

3. Taking a section with slice

slice(start, end) returns a new array holding the elements from index start up to but not including end - it takes end - start elements, leaving out the one at position end:

const dailyRevenue = [500000, 720000, 610000, 830000, 940000, 1200000, 990000];
console.log(dailyRevenue.slice(0, 3));
console.log(dailyRevenue.slice(-2));
console.log(dailyRevenue.length);
[
  500000,
  720000,
  610000
]
[
  1200000,
  990000
]
7
  • slice(0, 3) - the first three days of the week: indexes 0, 1, 2.
  • slice(-2) - negative indexes count from the end: the two most recent days. Omitting the end parameter takes everything to the end of the array.
  • The last line is the most important point: the original array still has all 7 elements intact. slice never touches the original - it cuts a copy.

Omit both parameters and slice() copies the whole array - the standard way to modify a list while leaving the original intact:

const dailyRevenue = [500000, 720000, 610000];
const draft = dailyRevenue.slice();
draft.push(999999);
console.log(dailyRevenue.length);
console.log(draft.length);
3
4

JavaScript also has a method with a nearly identical name, splice - it modifies the original array in place and its parameters mean something entirely different, making the two very easy to confuse; this course never uses it, slice is all you need.

Key points

Distinguish methods that modify the original from methods that return a new array. push/pop modify in place; slice cuts a copy, leaving the original intact. Confusing slice with splice (which modifies in place) is a hard bug to find - this course uses slice only.

const does not make an array immutable. It only forbids reassigning the variable; the array's contents can still be push-ed and pop-ped freely.

indexOf returns -1 when nothing is found, not undefined. When a yes/no answer is all you need, includes states the intent more clearly - and both are case-sensitive.

lessons.title: map transform every element
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 29: map transform every element

theory.contentHtml:
Converting a column from dong to thousands of dong, pulling the amount column out of an order list, computing the line total on an invoice - all three are the same job: run through an array, transform each element, collect the results. JavaScript has a dedicated method for that class of work, and it is called map.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. The for loop works, but repeats itself
  2. map: transform every element
  3. Pulling one field out of a list of records
  4. Key points

1. The for loop works, but repeats itself

Converting a revenue column from dong to thousands of dong with for...of:

const revenuesVnd = [1200000, 950000, 1830000];
const revenuesThousand = [];
for (const revenue of revenuesVnd) {
  revenuesThousand.push(revenue / 1000);
}
console.log(revenuesThousand);
[
  1200,
  950,
  1830
]

It runs correctly, but look closer: of the 4 lines, 3 are scaffolding - create an empty array, loop, push. The only part carrying meaning is revenue / 1000. Every time you transform a column, you copy that same scaffolding and swap out one expression. When something repeats that literally, the language usually has it packaged.

2. map: transform every element

map takes a function, applies it to every element, and returns a new array of the results:

const revenuesVnd = [1200000, 950000, 1830000];
const revenuesThousand = revenuesVnd.map((revenue) => revenue / 1000);
console.log(revenuesThousand);
console.log(revenuesVnd);
[
  1200,
  950,
  1830
]
[
  1200000,
  950000,
  1830000
]

Four lines of scaffolding become one, and the meaningful part - (revenue) => revenue / 1000 - sits right on the surface. The function passed to map is the arrow function from the previous module, in a new role: an argument to a method (this role is called a callback). The second console.log confirms an important property: the original array is unchanged - map always returns a new array.

3. Pulling one field out of a list of records

The second thing map does daily: pulling one field out of a list of records. Each element below is an object - a record with named fields, covered properly in "Objects: records with named fields"; for now, all you need is that order.amount reads the record's amount field:

const orders = [
  { id: 1, region: "North", amount: 1200000 },
  { id: 2, region: "South", amount: 950000 },
  { id: 3, region: "North", amount: 1830000 },
];
const amounts = orders.map((order) => order.amount);
console.log(amounts);
[
  1200000,
  950000,
  1830000
]

From a 3-row × 3-column "table", map extracts exactly the amount column. Notice: 3 elements in, exactly 3 elements out - map never adds or removes, it only reshapes each element.

The callback receives the whole record, so it can compute a derived column out of several fields - something the source data does not contain:

const lines = [
  { product: "Keyboard", unitPrice: 500000, quantity: 2 },
  { product: "Monitor", unitPrice: 3200000, quantity: 1 },
];
const lineTotals = lines.map((line) => line.unitPrice * line.quantity);
console.log(lineTotals);
[
  1000000,
  3200000
]

Key points

map reshapes each element and keeps the count. However many elements go in, exactly that many come out - map never adds or removes.

map returns a new array and leaves the original intact. Quite unlike the previous lesson's push/pop, which write straight into the existing array.

The callback receives the whole element, not just one field. That is how it computes derived columns - unit price times quantity, say - rather than only copying a field that already exists.

lessons.title: filter select data by condition
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 31: filter select data by condition

theory.contentHtml:
"Working with arrays" ended with a manual filter: empty array, loop, if, push. Just as map packages the transforming job, JavaScript has filter for the selecting job - and because both return arrays, they connect into a single data-processing pipeline.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. filter: keep the elements that qualify
  2. Chaining filter and map
  3. Familiar thinking from SQL and Python
  4. Key points

1. filter: keep the elements that qualify

filter takes a function just like map, but that function must return true/false - the elements that produce true are kept in the result:

const dailyRevenue = [500000, 1250000, 610000, 1830000];
const bigDays = dailyRevenue.filter((revenue) => revenue >= 1000000);
console.log(bigDays);
[
  1250000,
  1830000
]

Exactly the manual filter from "Working with arrays", packed into one line. With a list of records, the condition reads almost like plain speech:

const orders = [
  { id: 1, status: "completed", amount: 1200000 },
  { id: 2, status: "pending", amount: 950000 },
  { id: 3, status: "completed", amount: 400000 },
  { id: 4, status: "cancelled", amount: 1830000 },
];
const completedOrders = orders.filter((order) => order.status === "completed");
console.log(JSON.stringify(completedOrders));
[{"id":1,"status":"completed","amount":1200000},{"id":3,"status":"completed","amount":400000}]

The mirror image of map: the element count can shrink (4 down to 2), but each element is kept fully intact - filter never edits a record's contents, it only decides keep-or-drop. Memorize this symmetric pair and you can tell the two methods apart forever: map changes the elements and keeps the count; filter changes the count and keeps the elements.

The most common beginner mistake: using map to filter. orders.map((order) => order.status === "completed") does not return the orders - it returns [true, false, true, false], because map takes the function's result as the new element. Need to keep/drop elements → filter; need to transform elements → map.

2. Chaining filter and map

Since both return arrays, the result of one method can call the next. A real business question: "revenue (in thousands of dong) of the completed orders":

const orders = [
  { id: 1, status: "completed", amount: 1200000 },
  { id: 2, status: "pending", amount: 950000 },
  { id: 3, status: "completed", amount: 400000 },
  { id: 4, status: "cancelled", amount: 1830000 },
];
const completedThousands = orders
  .filter((order) => order.status === "completed")
  .map((order) => order.amount / 1000);
console.log(completedThousands);
[
  1200,
  400
]

Read the chain top to bottom like a pipeline: 4 orders → filtered down to the 2 completed ones → each turned into a number in thousands. The order is deliberate: filter first, transform after, so the map step only works on elements that will actually be used. The layout convention above - one step per line, leading dot - is the common style: however many steps the chain grows to, each stage stays readable.

3. Familiar thinking from SQL and Python

If you have written SQL, these two methods are not new - only renamed. filter plays exactly the role of the WHERE clause: deciding which rows survive. map plays the role of the expression list after SELECT: deciding what shape each surviving row appears in - choosing columns, converting units, computing derived columns. The filter-then-map chain in section 2 is a SELECT ... WHERE ... written vertically. And if Python is your home, these are the two halves of a list comprehension: the leading expression is the map, the trailing if clause is the filter - Python fuses the two halves into one syntax, JavaScript splits them into two chainable methods, but the data operation underneath is one and the same.

Key points

map changes the elements and keeps the count; filter changes the count and keeps the elements. This symmetric pair is the entire difference - know it and you pick the right tool in a second.

Using map to filter is the classic mistake: the result is an array of true/false, not an array of elements. The function you pass to filter is the one that returns a condition.

Both return new arrays and leave the original intact - which is exactly why they chain. That is the difference from the push/pop in "Working with arrays".

Filter first, transform after. The filter → map chain both matches how business questions are phrased and avoids transforming elements that are about to be dropped.

lessons.title: reduce fold an array into one number
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 33: reduce fold an array into one number

theory.contentHtml:
map and filter take an array and return an array. But plenty of business questions do not want an array - they want one number: what is this month's total revenue, what was the largest order. The tool for the "fold a whole array into one value" class of work is reduce.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. From an array to a single value
  2. How reduce runs: the accumulator
  3. Total revenue from a list of orders
  4. Key points

1. From an array to a single value

You already summed with for...of in the "Arrays: lists of values" lesson:

const amounts = [1200000, 950000, 1830000, 700000];
let total = 0;
for (const amount of amounts) {
  total = total + amount;
}
console.log(total);
4680000

Seen through the map lesson's eyes: 3 lines of scaffolding (initialize total, loop, reassign), 1 meaningful expression (total + amount). reduce packages exactly this pattern:

const amounts = [1200000, 950000, 1830000, 700000];
const total = amounts.reduce((sum, amount) => sum + amount, 0);
console.log(total);
4680000

2. How reduce runs: the accumulator

reduce takes two things: a function and an initial value (the trailing 0). This time the function has two parameters - unlike map/filter with one:

  • sum - the accumulator: the folded result so far. On the first pass, it receives the initial value 0.
  • amount - the element being visited, as in map/filter.

On every pass, the function returns the new accumulated value, and that value is passed in as sum on the next pass. Traced by hand on the array above:

sum = 0        (initial value)
sum = 0       + 1200000 = 1200000
sum = 1200000 + 950000  = 2150000
sum = 2150000 + 1830000 = 3980000
sum = 3980000 + 700000  = 4680000   ← returned result

Line it up against the for loop in section 1: sum is the total variable, the initial value 0 is the let total = 0 line, and the returned expression is the assignment inside the loop body. reduce does nothing a for loop cannot - it merely compresses the "accumulate" pattern into one expression.

The initial value also settles an edge case that is easy to forget: the empty array. [].reduce((sum, amount) => sum + amount, 0) returns 0 - the function never runs, and the initial value goes straight out as the result. Leave the initial value off, and an empty array makes reduce throw an error - which is why this course always writes reduce with both arguments.

3. Total revenue from a list of orders

Real data is rarely a bare array of numbers - usually it is a list of records. The accumulator sums one field of each record:

const orders = [
  { id: 1, region: "North", amount: 1200000 },
  { id: 2, region: "South", amount: 950000 },
  { id: 3, region: "North", amount: 1830000 },
];
const totalRevenue = orders.reduce((sum, order) => sum + order.amount, 0);
console.log(totalRevenue);
3980000

Combined with filter it completes the pipeline - "total revenue of the completed orders":

const orders = [
  { id: 1, status: "completed", amount: 1200000 },
  { id: 2, status: "pending", amount: 950000 },
  { id: 3, status: "completed", amount: 400000 },
];
const completedRevenue = orders
  .filter((order) => order.status === "completed")
  .reduce((sum, order) => sum + order.amount, 0);
console.log(completedRevenue);
1600000

Key points

reduce = the "accumulate over a loop" pattern, compressed. The accumulator is the running variable, the initial value is the initialization line, and the function's return value is the per-pass assignment. Can't parse a reduce? Translate it back into its for loop.

Always pass an initial value. Without it, an empty array makes reduce throw instead of returning a sensible empty result.

reduce's callback has two parameters; map/filter have one. The first is the result folded so far, the second is the element being visited - swap the two and you get a meaningless number.

lessons.title: reduce by group an object accumulator
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 34: reduce by group an object accumulator

theory.contentHtml:
The previous lesson folded a whole array into one number. But the question that comes up more often in data work is folding by group: how many orders per region, how much revenue per category. The accumulator does not have to be a number - make it a table and reduce answers that entire class of question. This lesson is also frank about when not to use reduce.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Counting by group with an object
  2. When to go back to a for loop
  3. The SUM and GROUP BY connection
  4. Key points

1. Counting by group with an object

Make the accumulator an object - a key–value record, covered properly in "Objects: records with named fields"; for now picture it as a tally board - and reduce answers "how many orders per region":

const orders = [
  { id: 1, region: "North" },
  { id: 2, region: "South" },
  { id: 3, region: "North" },
  { id: 4, region: "North" },
];
const countByRegion = orders.reduce((counts, order) => {
  if (counts[order.region] === undefined) {
    counts[order.region] = 0;
  }
  counts[order.region] = counts[order.region] + 1;
  return counts;
}, {});
console.log(JSON.stringify(countByRegion));
{"North":3,"South":1}

The initial value is {} - an empty tally board. Each pass: if the region has no slot yet, open one at 0, then add 1 to that region's slot. Because the function body is now a block in curly braces (no longer a one-line expression), you must write return counts yourself - an arrow function only returns implicitly when its body is a brace-less expression.

Forgetting the return is mistake number one with block-bodied reduce:

// Wrong - the block body never returns the accumulator
const countByRegion = orders.reduce((counts, order) => {
  counts[order.region] = (counts[order.region] || 0) + 1;
}, {});

From the second pass on, counts receives the previous pass's return value - that is, undefined - and the program dies with a confusing message deep inside the callback. When reduce reports "cannot read properties of undefined", check the return first.

2. When to go back to a for loop

Compare two ways of writing the same tally:

const orders = [
  { id: 1, region: "North" },
  { id: 2, region: "South" },
  { id: 3, region: "North" },
  { id: 4, region: "North" },
];
const countByRegion = {};
for (const order of orders) {
  if (countByRegion[order.region] === undefined) {
    countByRegion[order.region] = 0;
  }
  countByRegion[order.region] = countByRegion[order.region] + 1;
}
console.log(JSON.stringify(countByRegion));
{"North":3,"South":1}

The for...of version is barely longer, and easier to read: no accumulator passed invisibly between passes, no return to forget, and the countByRegion variable stays in plain sight from start to finish. This is something many tutorials avoid saying: reduce with an object accumulator is often harder to read than the equivalent loop.

This course's pragmatic rule:

  • Folding to a simple value (sum, count, max) with a one-line expression → reduce is concise and idiomatic.
  • Object accumulator, brace-bodied function, logic with if → consider for...of. Readable code beats code that "looks pro".

Choosing a for loop when it is clearer is not a step backwards - your code reviewer will thank you.

3. The SUM and GROUP BY connection

Set the two reduce lessons next to the query language you know: the revenue total in the previous lesson is SUM over a column - with a filter in front, it is SUM with a WHERE. And the per-region tally in section 1 is GROUP BY region followed by a count per group: each key of the result object is a group, and its value is that group's aggregate. The difference worth remembering: SQL lets you declare the result you want and works out how to compute it, while reduce makes you assemble the aggregation table step by step with your own hands - which is why the SQL version of the same question is usually shorter. In exchange, reduce runs anywhere JavaScript runs, directly on data an API just returned, with no need to load it into a database first.

Key points

The accumulator does not have to be a number. Make it {} and each key of the result object becomes a group - that is group aggregation with no library at all.

A brace-bodied function must return the accumulator itself. Forget it → the next pass receives undefined → "cannot read properties of undefined" right inside the callback.

reduce is not a skill meter. Simple folds → reduce; complicated folding logic → for...of is usually easier to read, and readability wins.

lessons.title: Objects records with named fields
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 36: Objects records with named fields

theory.contentHtml:
For several lessons now, records like { id: 1, region: "North" } have appeared with a promise of "covered properly later". This lesson pays that debt: the object - JavaScript's named-field record structure. An array answers "which position", an object answers "which name", and putting the two together produces the data shape you meet most often: an array of records.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Objects: records with named fields
  2. Dot access and bracket access
  3. Object.keys and Object.values
  4. Key points

1. Objects: records with named fields

An object is written with curly braces, holding name: value pairs:

const product = {
  name: "Wireless Mouse",
  category: "Electronics",
  price: 350000,
  inStock: true,
};
console.log(product.name);
console.log(product.price);
Wireless Mouse
350000

In a data person's head, an object is one row of a table: field names are column names, values are the cells. A field takes any type of value - string, number, boolean, even another array or object nested inside. And an array of objects is the whole table: order lists, query results, API data all wear that shape - exactly what filter, map and reduce have been working on all module.

Assign into a field to change it or add it - an object declared with const can still have its contents modified, just like arrays in "Working with arrays":

const product = { name: "Wireless Mouse", price: 350000 };
product.price = 320000;
product.sku = "WM-2041";
console.log(JSON.stringify(product));
{"name":"Wireless Mouse","price":320000,"sku":"WM-2041"}

2. Dot access and bracket access

The dot, product.price, is the everyday way to read. But it has one important limit: what follows the dot must be a field name written literally in the code. When the field name lives in a variable - extremely common when writing generic data-handling functions - you need square brackets:

const row = { region: "North", amount: 1200000 };
const field = "amount";
console.log(row[field]);
console.log(row["region"]);
console.log(row.field);
1200000
North
undefined

Read the three result lines carefully:

  • row[field] - square brackets evaluate the expression inside first: field is "amount", so this reads the amount field. This is the only way when the field name is only known at runtime.
  • row["region"] - brackets with a literal string are also valid, equivalent to row.region.
  • row.field - the dot takes things literally: it looks for a field actually named field, finds none, and returns undefined. No error, no warning - exactly like out-of-range array access.

That last point deserves a pause: a typo in a field name also just returns a silent undefined (row.amuont, say). With real data, this is the single most common source of undefined - check the spelling of your field names before you suspect the data.

3. Object.keys and Object.values

Two utility functions turn an object back into arrays - for counting, iterating, or further folding:

const revenueByRegion = { North: 3030000, South: 950000, Central: 1100000 };
console.log(Object.keys(revenueByRegion));
console.log(Object.values(revenueByRegion));
console.log(Object.keys(revenueByRegion).length);
[
  "North",
  "South",
  "Central"
]
[
  3030000,
  950000,
  1100000
]
3
  • Object.keys(obj) - an array of the field names. Counting "how many regions" = the length of this array (objects have no .length of their own).
  • Object.values(obj) - an array of the values, and since it is an array, the entire toolkit of the last few lessons applies immediately:
const revenueByRegion = { North: 3030000, South: 950000, Central: 1100000 };
const total = Object.values(revenueByRegion).reduce((sum, value) => sum + value, 0);
console.log(total);
5080000

The loop closes: reduce folds an array of records into a per-group object, and Object.values opens the object back into an array for further folding.

Key points

An object is a record with named fields; an array of objects is a data table. The "array of objects" shape is the most important data shape in the course - filter/map/reduce are all designed around it.

Dot for literal field names; brackets for field names held in variables. row.field looks for a field literally named "field" - to use the value of the variable field, write row[field].

A misspelled field name returns a silent undefined, not an error. On an unexpected undefined: inspect the spelling of the field name first, suspect the data second.

lessons.title: JSON data leaving the program
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 37: JSON data leaving the program

theory.contentHtml:
The objects in the previous lesson live in the program's memory. But data has to travel: from a server to a browser, from one system to another, into a file. To travel, it must become text - and the dominant text format is JSON, born from the very object syntax you just learned.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. JSON: the format every API returns
  2. JSON.parse and JSON.stringify
  3. Reading a mock response
  4. Key points

1. JSON: the format every API returns

JSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation. A typical API response looks like this:

[{"id":1,"region":"North","amount":1200000},{"id":2,"region":"South","amount":950000}]

Familiar-looking - but JSON is a stricter format than JavaScript syntax, differing on four points people trip over:

  • Field names must be in double quotes: "region", not region.
  • Strings use double quotes only - single quotes are invalid.
  • No trailing comma after the last element.
  • Data only: numbers, strings, booleans, null, arrays, objects - no functions, no comments.

And the most important, most forgettable fact: the JSON you receive from an API is a string - a sequence of characters. Until it is converted, you cannot dot into any field of it.

2. JSON.parse and JSON.stringify

Two conversion functions, one per direction - memorize them by the direction the data flows:

  • JSON.parse(text): string → data. Use when receiving - reading an API response, reading a file.
  • JSON.stringify(data): data → string. Use when sending or saving - and when you want to print a whole structure.
const order = { id: 42, region: "North", amount: 1200000 };
const text = JSON.stringify(order);
console.log(text);
console.log(JSON.stringify(order, null, 2));
{"id":42,"region":"North","amount":1200000}
{
  "id": 42,
  "region": "North",
  "amount": 1200000
}

The one-line form is for machines; adding the two arguments null, 2 produces a 2-space-indented printout for humans - a habit worth having whenever you need a clear look at an unfamiliar structure before writing code against it.

The other direction:

const text = '{"id":42,"region":"North","amount":1200000}';
const order = JSON.parse(text);
console.log(order.amount * 2);
2400000

Before parse, text.amount is undefined - a string has no amount field. After parse, order is a real object and calculations work. One more sentence worth knowing: hand JSON.parse a string that is not valid JSON and it throws an error that stops the program - unlike the silent-undefined behavior you have met so far - so strings from external sources deserve a careful eye.

3. Reading a mock response

The full assembly: receive a JSON string (standing in for an API response - in this lesson it is a string written directly in the code), parse it, then answer a business question with the module's toolkit:

const apiResponse = '[{"id":1,"region":"North","amount":1200000},{"id":2,"region":"South","amount":950000},{"id":3,"region":"North","amount":1830000}]';

const orders = JSON.parse(apiResponse);
console.log(orders.length);

const northTotal = orders
  .filter((order) => order.region === "North")
  .reduce((sum, order) => sum + order.amount, 0);
console.log(northTotal);
3
3030000

This three-beat rhythm - receive a string → parse into an array of objects → filter/map/reduce - is the standard rhythm of every session with API data. This course does not yet teach calling an API (that requires asynchronous programming, which is out of scope), but the processing that happens once the data arrives is now fully in your hands.

Key points

parse string → data when receiving; stringify data → string when sending/saving. An API response is a string - parse it before dotting into fields.

JSON is stricter than JavaScript's own object syntax. Field names in double quotes, strings in double quotes only, no trailing comma, no functions and no comments.

JSON.parse throws when the string is broken. That is a welcome exception in a language that so often returns a silent undefined - the error surfaces right where the data comes in.

stringify with null, 2 gives a readable printout. Reach for it whenever you need to see an unfamiliar structure before writing code against it.

options.label: A
options.text: regions[1] is "North", because indexes start at 1

options.label: B
options.text: regions[1] is "South", and the last element is read with regions[regions.length - 1]

options.label: C
options.text: regions.length is 3, because the largest index is 3

options.label: D
options.text: regions[4] throws an error and stops the program

questions.explanation: Array indexes start at 0: regions[0] is "North", so regions[1] is "South" - (a) is wrong because counting from 1 is a spreadsheet habit, not JavaScript's. length counts the number of elements, not the largest index: this array has 4 elements so length is 4, while indexes run from 0 to 3 - (c) mixes those two ideas up, and it is precisely this off-by-one gap that makes the last element regions[regions.length - 1], exactly as (b) says. As for (d), it misdescribes how JavaScript reacts: out-of-range access like regions[4] does not throw - it silently returns undefined, and that value can drift into calculations below and produce a confusing result somewhere else. That is why the lesson advises: on an unexpected undefined, suspect your indexes first.

questions.prompt: From the array orders (each element a record { id, status, amount }), you need an array holding only the orders with amount >= 1000000 - each record kept fully intact. Which tool is right for the job?

options.label: A
options.text: map, because it applies a function to every element of the array

options.label: B
options.text: filter, because you need to keep the qualifying elements without modifying them

options.label: C
options.text: reduce, because this is an operation over the whole array

options.label: D
options.text: push, because the qualifying orders need to be added to a result array

questions.explanation: The requirement shows both hallmarks of a selection: the element count may shrink (only qualifying orders survive) and each element stays fully intact (still a { id, status, amount } record) - exactly filter's job (b), with a callback returning the condition (order) => order.amount >= 1000000. (a) is wrong because map does the opposite: it keeps the count and reshapes each element - using map with the condition above yields [true, false, ...], an array of booleans rather than orders, the classic mistake the lesson warned about. (c) is wrong because reduce is for folding a whole array into one value (a sum, a tally...), while here the result must be an array of records - it could be forced to work, but it is a sledgehammer for a nut and reads far worse. (d) is wrong because push is merely the act of appending to an array - it is one piece of the manual for...of + if + push version, not a complete tool for selection.

options.label: A
options.text: The minimum number of elements the array must have for reduce to run

options.label: B
options.text: The initial value of the accumulator sum, before the first element is visited

options.label: C
options.text: The index at which to start walking the array

options.label: D
options.text: A value added in after every element

questions.explanation: reduce takes two things: the callback and the accumulator's initial value. On the first pass, sum receives exactly this value (0), and then each pass's callback returns the new accumulated value passed on to the next pass: 0 → 500 → 700 → 1000 - so (b) is correct. It also settles the edge case: on an empty array the callback never runs and reduce returns the initial value directly (0) instead of throwing - which is why the lesson insists on always writing reduce with both arguments. (a) is wrong because no 'minimum element count' concept exists - with an initial value, even an empty array works fine. (c) is wrong because reduce always walks from the first element to the end; this argument has nothing to do with indexes. (d) is wrong because the thing added after each element is amount itself, in the sum + amount expression the callback defines - the 0 appears exactly once, at the start, and never again on later passes.

options.label: A
options.text: row.field

options.label: B
options.text: row[field]

options.label: C
options.text: row["field"]

options.label: D
options.text: row.amount()

questions.explanation: (b) is correct: square brackets evaluate the expression inside first - field is the string "amount", so row[field] is equivalent to row["amount"] and returns 1200000. It is the only way when the field name is known only at runtime (held in a variable, a function parameter...). (a) is wrong because the dot takes things literally: row.field looks for a field actually named field - the object has none, so it returns undefined, silently, with no error. (c) fails the same way: row["field"] passes the literal string "field" (not the value of the variable field), so it also hunts for a field named field and gets undefined - brackets only help when what is inside is an expression to evaluate; wrap it in quotes and it becomes a fixed string, no different from the dot. (d) is wrong because amount is a number, not a function - adding parentheses is a function call, and calling something that is not a function throws a real error rather than merely returning undefined.

questions.prompt: An API returns the string '{"region":"North","amount":1200000}' and you need to read the amount value for a calculation. What is the correct first step?

options.label: A
options.text: Run the string through JSON.stringify to turn it into an object

options.label: B
options.text: Run the string through JSON.parse to get an object, then read that object's amount field

options.label: C
options.text: Dot .amount directly on the string, since the string already holds the JSON content

options.label: D
options.text: Cut the string apart by character positions to extract the number

questions.explanation: Memorize by the direction the data flows: `parse` = string → data (used when *receiving*), `stringify` = data → string (used when *sending/saving*). Data arriving from an API is a string of characters, so the correct first step is JSON.parse to rebuild the object, after which .amount works normally - (b) is correct. (a) points the wrong way: JSON.stringify takes data and produces a string - feed it a string and you just get that string wrapped in another layer of quotes, further from the goal. (c) is wrong because a string has no amount field - it is only a character sequence that happens to look like an object; .amount on a string returns a silent undefined. (d) could in theory dig the number out, but it is the wrong trade: brittle against every small change in the data (an added field, reordered fields, a negative number...), while JSON.parse is the tool built for exactly this job and reports a clear error when the string is invalid.

options.label: A
options.text: ["Keyboard","Monitor"]

options.label: B
options.text: ["Monitor"]

options.label: C
options.text: [{"name":"Keyboard","price":500000},{"name":"Monitor","price":3200000}]

options.label: D
options.text: ["Keyboard","Monitor","Mouse"]

questions.explanation: Read the chain top to bottom like a pipeline. The filter step keeps products with price >= 500000: Keyboard costs exactly 500000 - the comparison is >=, so it is kept - and so is Monitor (3200000); Mouse (200000) is dropped. The map step turns each surviving record into just its name field, giving ["Keyboard","Monitor"] - (a) is correct. (b) is what you get if the comparison were > instead of >= - missing one equals sign is a very human misread, and exactly why practice problems spell out whether "X or more" includes the boundary. (c) is the result of stopping after `filter` and forgetting the map step: the records still carry both name and price. (d) is the result of skipping the `filter`: all three names appear, including Mouse below the threshold. The last two options echo the core symmetric pair: filter changes the count and keeps the elements; map changes the elements and keeps the count.

lessons.title: Normalizing strings trim and lower case
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 40: Normalizing strings trim and lower case

theory.contentHtml:
Open the product-name column of a hand-entered orders file and this is what you will find: " Coffee Beans 500g", "coffee beans 500G ", "COFFEE BEANS 500g" - one product, three spellings. Count orders per product on that data and you get three rows instead of one. This lesson deals with exactly that pain: bringing a text column into one consistent form before you count it.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Three spellings, three different strings
  2. trim and toLowerCase
  3. Normalizing a whole column
  4. Key points

1. Three spellings, three different strings

Data born from manual entry is rarely clean. People add stray spaces, switch between upper and lower case - and to the machine, every variant is a completely different string:

const first = "  Coffee Beans 500g";
const second = "COFFEE BEANS 500g";
console.log(first === second);
false

false - even though any human reader sees one product. Every comparison, count, and grouping matches strings character by character, so before any analysis, a text column has to be brought into one consistent form. The two methods below do most of that work.

2. trim and toLowerCase

trim() returns a copy with all whitespace removed from the start and the end of the string - whitespace between words is kept. toLowerCase() converts the whole string to lower case (the opposite direction is toUpperCase()):

const rawName = "  Coffee Beans 500g  ";
console.log(rawName.trim());
console.log(rawName.length);
console.log(rawName.trim().length);
console.log("Green TEA".toLowerCase());
console.log("TEA" === "tea");
Coffee Beans 500g
21
17
green tea
false

Note the line printing 21: the original string is unchanged. In JavaScript, strings are immutable - no method can edit a string in place; every one of them returns a new string. Forgetting to assign the result back is a classic bug:

let productName = "  Coffee Beans  ";
productName.trim();          // result thrown away - productName still has spaces
console.log(productName.length);  // 16: the spaces are still there
productName = productName.trim(); // correct: assign the result back
console.log(productName.length);  // 12: the trimmed value is kept

Stray whitespace is dangerous precisely because your eyes cannot see it in a report - you just see two identical-looking "Coffee Beans" rows that the machine insists are different. As for case, the common working convention among data people is to lowercase a text column before comparing or grouping it: not because lowercase is "more correct", but because you need one consistent form, and lowercase is the least controversial choice.

3. Normalizing a whole column

Combine the two methods into one normalizing function, then apply it to the whole column with map:

function normalizeName(rawName) {
  return rawName.trim().toLowerCase();
}

const rawNames = ["  Coffee Beans 500g", "coffee beans 500G ", "COFFEE BEANS 500g"];
console.log(JSON.stringify(rawNames.map(normalizeName)));
["coffee beans 500g","coffee beans 500g","coffee beans 500g"]

The three variants are now one single string - counting, grouping, and comparing all produce correct results. Look at how rawName.trim().toLowerCase() is written: because each method returns a new string, calls can be chained (method chaining) - trim() runs first and returns the trimmed string, toLowerCase() then runs on that result. The chain reads left to right, in exactly the order it executes.

The practice exercise that comes next is this very problem in full: cleaning an entire column, empty cells included.

Key points

Strings are immutable - trim, toLowerCase and every other string method return a new string rather than editing the old one. Forget to assign the result back and you have cleaned the data... and thrown the result away.

Every string comparison is case-sensitive and counts whitespace. "TEA", "tea", and " tea" are three different values.

Normalize before comparing, counting, or grouping. The trim + toLowerCase pair handles most hand-entered data; wrap it in a function and map it over the whole column.

lessons.title: Searching, replacing and slicing strings
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 42: Searching, replacing and slicing strings

theory.contentHtml:
Once a text column is normalized, the next step is usually asking it a few questions: is this row a coffee product, which year does this order id belong to, what number does the price text "1.250.000" become once the dots are gone. The three groups of methods in this lesson answer exactly those three questions - search, replace, and slice.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. includes and startsWith: does the string contain it
  2. replace and replaceAll
  3. slice and padStart
  4. Key points

1. includes and startsWith: does the string contain it

Two methods that return true/false, used to filter rows by string content:

  • includes(part) - whether the string contains part anywhere.
  • startsWith(part) - whether the string begins with part.
const description = "Organic Coffee Beans 500g";
console.log(description.includes("Coffee"));
console.log(description.includes("coffee"));
console.log(description.startsWith("Organic"));
true
false
true

The second line deserves attention: both methods are case-sensitive. "Coffee" is in the string, "coffee" is not. So when filtering real data, normalize first, then check:

const productNames = ["Coffee Beans 500g", "Instant coffee box", "Green Tea 100g"];
const coffeeProducts = productNames.filter((name) => name.toLowerCase().includes("coffee"));
console.log(JSON.stringify(coffeeProducts));
["Coffee Beans 500g","Instant coffee box"]

Without normalizing, "Instant coffee box" slips through the net because of its lowercase c. startsWith is most useful with structured codes: order ids starting with "ORD-", region codes starting with "VN-".

2. replace and replaceAll

replace(a, b) replaces a with b - but only the first occurrence. To replace them all, use replaceAll(a, b). A real-life example: Vietnamese-style price text "1.250.000" needs every dot removed before it can become a number:

const priceText = "1.250.000";
console.log(priceText.replace(".", ""));
console.log(priceText.replaceAll(".", ""));
console.log(Number(priceText.replaceAll(".", "")));
1250.000
1250000
1250000

The first line is the trap: replace only removes the first dot, producing "1250.000" - feed that into Number() and you get 1250 (the remaining dot is read as a decimal point), a value wrong by a factor of one thousand with no error anywhere. This class of bug is hard to trace because the program runs smoothly; only the number on the report is wrong.

3. slice and padStart

slice(start, end) returns the piece from position start up to but not including position end. Positions count from 0; negative positions count from the end. padStart(length, char) works the other way - it pads char onto the front of the string until it reaches length:

const orderId = "ORD-2026-000123";
console.log(orderId.slice(0, 3));
console.log(orderId.slice(-6));

const orderDate = "2026-01-15";
console.log(orderDate.slice(5, 7));

console.log(String(7).padStart(3, "0"));
ORD
000123
01
007

Pulling the month out of a YYYY-MM-DD date string to group revenue by month is everyday data work, and cutting like this works because the data has a fixed structure - the month always sits at characters 6 and 7. For data without fixed positions, use split - the main tool of the CSV lessons just ahead.

Two things to note about padStart: it is a string method, so a number must go through String(...) first; and if the string is already at or beyond length, it is returned unchanged, never truncated. Its most familiar uses are zero-padding codes ("007", matching product codes like SP007) and right-aligning a number column in the console for a quick visual check.

Key points

includes and startsWith are case-sensitive. With real data, normalize first and check second, or you lose exactly the rows people typed differently.

replace only replaces the first occurrence. Replacing every occurrence is replaceAll's job. Mixing the two up on money data like "1.250.000" means being wrong by a factor of one thousand with no error message.

slice(start, end) excludes position end, and positions count from 0. Negative positions count from the end - slice(-6) takes the last 6 characters. Cutting by position only works when the data has a fixed structure.

lessons.title: split and join strings to arrays and back
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 44: split and join strings to arrays and back

theory.contentHtml:
A CSV file - the most common tabular format a data person receives - is really just one long string: columns separated by commas, rows separated by newline characters. This lesson covers the two core moves for working with it: splitting a string into an array, and joining an array back into a string.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. CSV is a string before it is a table
  2. Splitting with split: rows and columns
  3. Joining back with join
  4. Key points

1. CSV is a string before it is a table

Open a .csv file in a plain text editor (not Excel) and you see its true form:

product,price
Coffee Beans,120000
Green Tea,85000

No cells, no table - just characters. CSV stands for comma-separated values: values separated by commas. The "table" you see in Excel exists because the software interprets this string. When a program reads such a file, what it receives is also a string - and to compute on it, you have to turn it into a data structure yourself.

2. Splitting with split: rows and columns

split(separator) cuts the string at every occurrence of separator and returns an array of the pieces. A whole CSV file is one string in which rows are separated by the newline character, written "\n" (one special character, not the two characters \ and n) - so reading CSV comes down to two splits:

const csvText = "product,price\nCoffee Beans,120000\nGreen Tea,85000";
const lines = csvText.split("\n");
console.log(lines.length);
console.log(lines[0]);

const columns = lines[1].split(",");
console.log(JSON.stringify(columns));
console.log(columns[0]);
3
product,price
["Coffee Beans","120000"]
Coffee Beans

Two things to take away from that output. First, lines[0] is the header row: column names, not data - processing has to set it aside, usually with slice(1) on the array of lines. Skip that step and "sum the price column" adds the string "price" into the total. Second, every element is a string, including "120000" which looks like a number: split does not guess data types, it only cuts. The next lesson deals with types.

The separator is whatever the real data uses: a file using semicolons needs split(";"), tabs need split("\t").

3. Joining back with join

join(separator) is the reverse of split: it connects the array's elements into one string, inserting separator between them:

const columns = ["Coffee Beans", "120000", "25"];
console.log(columns.join(","));
console.log(columns.join(" | "));
Coffee Beans,120000,25
Coffee Beans | 120000 | 25

The first line reproduces the original CSV line exactly - split then join with the same separator is a round trip. Practical uses: exporting data back to CSV after fixing it, or join(" | ") to print a row for a human to eyeball.

The split/join pair is the founding mindset of all text data processing: split into an array, process with array tools, join back into a string. The middle part - processing with array tools - is the map, filter and reduce you learned in the previous module.

Key points

Reading CSV is two splits: split("\n") into lines, then split(",") on each line into columns.

split always returns an array of STRINGS. "120000" looks like a number but is not one yet - converting types is a separate job, handled in the next lesson.

The first line of a CSV file is the header, not data. Drop it with slice(1) before processing, or the column names get counted as a data row.

join is the reverse of split. Split to process with array tools, join to write the result back out - that is the frame of all reading and writing of text data.

lessons.title: From CSV lines to typed records
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 45: From CSV lines to typed records

theory.contentHtml:
Splitting gets you an array of strings - which you still cannot compute on. This lesson covers the rest of the way: converting number columns to real numbers, then wrapping each line into an object with named fields, so every array skill you have learned applies to real file data.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Turning number columns into real numbers with Number
  2. The full parse: an array of objects
  3. The limits: when commas live inside the data
  4. Key points

1. Turning number columns into real numbers with Number

As the previous lesson warned: after split, the price column is the string "120000", not yet a number. Arithmetic on strings behaves very differently:

const priceText = "120000";
console.log(Number(priceText) + 5000);
console.log(priceText + 5000);
console.log(Number("abc"));
125000
1200005000
NaN

Read each line carefully:

  • Number("120000") + 5000 → 125000 - what you meant.
  • "120000" + 5000 → "1200005000" - + with a string means concatenation, not addition. No error, no warning, just a wrong result.
  • Number("abc") → NaN (Not a Number) - a string that cannot be read as a number. NaN is not a program-stopping error: it silently spreads into every calculation it touches (NaN + 5 is still NaN), and your final revenue total ends up as NaN. Checking with Number.isNaN(value) right after converting is a self-defense habit with real data - where a price column occasionally contains "N/A" or an empty cell.

The short rule: after split, any column you will compute on goes through Number() immediately.

2. The full parse: an array of objects

Putting it all together: split into lines, drop the header, split each line into columns, convert the number column - with map doing it for every line at once:

const csvText = "product,price\nCoffee Beans,120000\nGreen Tea,85000\nMilk,32000";
const dataLines = csvText.split("\n").slice(1);

const products = dataLines.map((line) => {
  const columns = line.split(",");
  return { name: columns[0], price: Number(columns[1]) };
});

console.log(JSON.stringify(products[0]));
console.log(products.length);
{"name":"Coffee Beans","price":120000}
3

From a raw string, you now have products - an array of objects in exactly the shape you have worked with throughout the previous modules: filter for products under 100000, map to pull out the name column, reduce to sum prices. This is the payoff moment of the whole module: every array skill you have learned applies to real file data the instant the parse is done.

These 6 lines are the skeleton of every hand-written CSV reader. Understand them and you can read a good share of real-world data-processing scripts.

3. The limits: when commas live inside the data

An honest word about the limits of the approach above. Real CSV allows values that contain commas, in which case the value is wrapped in double quotes:

// This line has TWO columns, but split(",") cuts it into THREE pieces:
const line = '"Espresso, dark roast",180000';
console.log(line.split(","));
// -> [""Espresso", " dark roast"", "180000"] (3 pieces)

split(",") does not understand quotes - it cuts at every comma, including the one inside the product name. Handling the full CSV standard (quotes, nested quotes, newlines inside cells) is what parser libraries are for - in practice you will use one rather than writing your own.

So why learn this at all? Two reasons. One: plenty of simple text data (logs, internal exports, data whose format you control) has no commas inside values - splitting it yourself is sufficient and fast. Two: the split-convert-wrap mindset underpins all text data work, even when the splitting is later done by a library.

Key points

After split, any column used in calculations must go through Number(). Remember that "text" + number concatenates rather than adds - no error, just a wrong figure.

Number() returns NaN on failure, not an error. NaN spreads silently into every downstream calculation. A revenue total of NaN almost certainly means a non-numeric cell slipped in - check with Number.isNaN.

Once parsed, every array tool is available. An array of objects with named fields is exactly the shape map/filter/reduce were built for.

split(",") cannot handle commas inside quoted fields. For files whose format you do not control, use a parser library. This part teaches the split-join mindset, not how to write a complete parser.

lessons.title: Dates creating a Date and reading its parts
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 47: Dates creating a Date and reading its parts

theory.contentHtml:
A date column shows up in almost every dataset: order date, delivery date, signup date. But "2026-01-15" read from a file is only a string - to know which weekday it falls on, or which month to group revenue under, you need JavaScript's Date object. This lesson covers creating a Date and reading its parts, along with its most famous trap.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Creating a date from an ISO string
  2. Reading the parts of a date
  3. The biggest trap: getMonth counts from 0
  4. Key points

1. Creating a date from an ISO string

The standard date format in data is ISO 8601: YYYY-MM-DD - year first, then month, then day, e.g. "2026-01-15". It is the format you should expect (and produce) in every data file. Pass an ISO string to new Date(...) to create a date object:

const orderDate = new Date("2026-01-15T00:00:00");
console.log(orderDate.getFullYear());
2026

Unlike the string "2026-01-15", which is just a sequence of characters, a Date object knows it is a moment in time: you can ask it for the year, the month, the weekday, and subtract it from another date.

About the T00:00:00 tail: it says explicitly "midnight in the timezone of the machine running the code". Writing the bare form new Date("2026-01-15") is also valid but is read as midnight UTC (universal time) - a subtle difference that becomes a real trap in the next lesson. The rule used throughout this course: when reading date parts, write it with T00:00:00; the next lesson covers the other half, producing a date string.

2. Reading the parts of a date

The get* family reads the individual parts of a Date:

const orderDate = new Date("2026-01-15T00:00:00");
console.log(orderDate.getFullYear());
console.log(orderDate.getDate());
console.log(orderDate.getDay());
2026
15
4
  • getFullYear() → the full 4-digit year.
  • getDate() → the day of the month, 1–31.
  • getDay() → the day of the week, 0–6, where 0 is Sunday, 1 is Monday... 4 means 2026-01-15 falls on a Thursday.

The getDate/getDay pair is confusable to an inexcusable degree: getDate is the day of the month, getDay is the day of the week. For data people, getDay() powers a very common class of questions: "how does weekend revenue compare to weekdays?" - filtering orders where getDay() is 0 or 6 is half the job.

3. The biggest trap: getMonth counts from 0

Read this output carefully before reading the explanation:

const orderDate = new Date("2026-03-10T00:00:00");
console.log(orderDate.getMonth());
console.log(orderDate.getMonth() + 1);
2
3

A March order, and getMonth() returns 2. Not a bug: getMonth counts months from 0 - January is 0, March is 2, December is 11. This is Date's most famous trap, and it bites data people harder than anyone, from both directions:

  • Filtering: "get March orders" is correctly written getMonth() === 2. Writing === 3 silently hands you April's data.
  • Displaying: putting getMonth() straight into a report shifts every number back one month. To print for humans, add 1: getMonth() + 1.

Neither direction produces any error - the program runs smoothly; only the report is a month off. Meanwhile getDate() counts from 1 as normal. The inconsistency is a historical legacy of the language that you simply live with: wherever you see getMonth, think "did I add 1?".

Key points

The ISO string YYYY-MM-DD is the standard date format in data. When reading its parts, create the Date with the T00:00:00 tail so midnight is measured in the running machine's timezone.

getMonth counts from 0 - March is 2. Filter against the number minus 1; add 1 when printing reports. Either way around, there is no error message - only figures shifted by a month.

getDate is the day of the month; getDay is the day of the week (0 = Sunday). Date's most confusable pair of names.

lessons.title: Comparing dates and producing date strings
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 48: Comparing dates and producing date strings

theory.contentHtml:
Once you can read the parts of a date, the next question is usually a comparison: was this order placed before or after that one, how many days until the customer came back. And once computed, the result has to go back out as a string to be saved to a file. This lesson handles both directions.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Comparing two dates with getTime
  2. Getting a YYYY-MM-DD string with toISOString
  3. Why this course never uses the current date and time
  4. Key points

1. Comparing two dates with getTime

getTime() turns a Date into a number: the count of milliseconds since 00:00 UTC on 1970-01-01 (the epoch). It sounds technical, but its value is simple: comparing numbers leaves no ambiguity:

const firstSeenMs = Date.parse("2026-01-05");
const lastSeenMs = Date.parse("2026-01-26");
const msPerDay = 1000 * 60 * 60 * 24;

console.log(firstSeenMs < lastSeenMs);
console.log((lastSeenMs - firstSeenMs) / msPerDay);
true
21

For date-only YYYY-MM-DD strings, Date.parse places both values at midnight UTC. Because both use one time scale without daylight-saving transitions, subtracting them and dividing by the milliseconds in a day correctly gives 21 calendar days.

Do not apply that formula blindly to two local-midnight values: across a daylight-saving transition, a local day can contain 23 or 25 hours. For elapsed time between timestamps that include a time and zone, keep the result in hours/minutes/seconds instead of forcing it into "calendar days".

And here is Date's second trap, on par with getMonth:

const a = new Date("2026-01-05T00:00:00");
const b = new Date("2026-01-05T00:00:00");
console.log(a === b);
console.log(a.getTime() === b.getTime());
false
true

Two Dates pointing at the same moment, yet === returns false - because Date is an object, and === checks whether both sides are the same object in memory, not whether they hold the same time. The iron rule: comparing dates means comparing their getTime() values - for equality, greater than, and less than alike.

2. Getting a YYYY-MM-DD string with toISOString

The reverse of new Date(string): getting a standard string out of a Date, to write into a file or name a report. toISOString() returns the full ISO string in UTC; slicing the first 10 characters gives YYYY-MM-DD:

const reportDate = new Date("2026-01-15");
console.log(reportDate.toISOString());
console.log(reportDate.toISOString().slice(0, 10));
2026-01-15T00:00:00.000Z
2026-01-15

Notice the well-matched pair here: a bare date string "2026-01-15" is parsed as UTC, and toISOString also prints in UTC (the trailing Z means UTC) - UTC in, UTC out, so the string you get back equals the original on every machine. Mixing the two paths breaks it:

// Mixing the two flavors is how a report silently loses one day:
const reportDate = new Date("2026-01-15"); // parsed as midnight UTC
console.log(reportDate.getDate());          // 15 on machines east of UTC, but 14 in New York

The bare string goes in as UTC, but getDate() reads in machine-local time - on a machine in a negative-offset timezone (the Americas) that moment is 23:00 the previous day, so it prints 14. Same line of code, two machines, two answers.

One final gift of ISO: YYYY-MM-DD strings sort alphabetically into correct chronological order, because the year comes first and every part is zero-padded. An array of ISO dates goes straight into sort().

3. Why this course never uses the current date and time

Date has two more familiar abilities that this course deliberately avoids in every runnable example:

// Both lines produce DIFFERENT results depending on when and where they run:
const now = new Date();                 // no argument = the current moment -> changes every run
console.log(now.toLocaleDateString());  // format follows the machine: "1/15/2026" vs "15/1/2026"

new Date() with no argument returns the current moment - one result today, another tomorrow. And toLocaleDateString() prints the date following the machine's local conventions: one machine shows 1/15/2026, another 15/1/2026.

Both have legitimate uses (timestamping logs, displaying to end users). But in analysis code, results that change with the machine and the day of the run are the enemy of reproducibility.

Key points

Compare instants with getTime(). === on two Date objects compares memory addresses and is always false for two distinct objects. For two date-only strings, parse both as UTC before dividing the millisecond gap into calendar days; do not use local midnights across a DST boundary.

Two in-out pairs - do not mix them: reading parts → new Date("...T00:00:00"); producing a YYYY-MM-DD string → new Date("2026-01-15") + toISOString().slice(0, 10). Mixing the paths makes reports drift a day depending on the machine's timezone.

ISO strings sort alphabetically into chronological order, so an array of YYYY-MM-DD dates goes straight into sort(). Meanwhile new Date() with no argument and toLocaleDateString give machine-dependent results - not for analysis code.
