lessons.title: Quiz Strings and real-world data
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 50: Quiz Strings and real-world data

questions.prompt: You count distinct products in a name column and one product shows up as two rows: "Coffee" and " Coffee". Why, and which processing step fixes the root cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The two strings are actually equal - the bug is elsewhere in the counting code

options.label: B
options.text: The leading space makes them differ character by character; strip whitespace from both ends of each value before counting

options.label: C
options.text: Both must be converted to upper case before the comparison can work at all

options.label: D
options.text: JavaScript strips whitespace automatically when comparing strings, so the problem is duplicated data

questions.explanation: String comparison in JavaScript matches character by character, so a single leading space is enough to make " Coffee" an entirely different value from "Coffee" - the counting code is not broken, it is faithfully reporting dirty data. The root-cause fix is to normalize before counting: strip whitespace from both ends of each value with trim(), usually together with toLowerCase() to handle case differences in the same pass. Converting everything to upper case would not save this case - upper or lower, the space is still sitting there, and " COFFEE" still differs from "COFFEE". And do not expect JavaScript to strip whitespace for you during comparison: to the language, a space is a character like any other - the danger is only that human eyes cannot see it on a report.

questions.prompt: A price in the file is the string "1.250.000" and you need every dot removed before converting it to a number. What does "1.250.000".replace(".", "") return?

options.label: A
options.text: "1250000" - all dots removed

options.label: B
options.text: "1250.000" - only the first dot removed

options.label: C
options.text: "1.250.000" - the original string, because replace found nothing

options.label: D
options.text: An error, because the string contains more than one dot

questions.explanation: replace(a, b) only replaces the first occurrence of a, so only the first dot disappears - the result is "1250.000". Removing all three dots takes replaceAll(".", "") - the behavior many people assume replace already has. Nor does replace give up or throw when it meets multiple matches: it does find a dot and does replace it, it just stops quietly after the first one - and that very quietness is what makes the trap hard to spot. The consequence is real: feed "1250.000" into Number() and you get 1250, because the leftover dot is read as a decimal point - a price wrong by a factor of one thousand with no error message anywhere. The original string itself is always unchanged (strings are immutable); what you get back is a new string with one dot removed.

questions.prompt: What does the expression "Coffee,120000,25".split(",") return?

options.label: A
options.text: A new string with the commas removed: "Coffee12000025"

options.label: B
options.text: An array of three strings: ["Coffee", "120000", "25"]

options.label: C
options.text: An array of one string and two numbers: ["Coffee", 120000, 25]

options.label: D
options.text: The number 3 - the count of columns in the line

questions.explanation: split(separator) cuts the string at every occurrence of the separator and returns an array of the pieces - here a three-element array, ["Coffee", "120000", "25"]. The easiest place to slip is the data type: every element is a string, including "120000" which merely looks like a number. split only cuts, it never guesses types, so "120000" + 5000 concatenates into "1200005000" instead of adding - making the price column a real number is your job, with Number() after splitting. split does not return a string with the commas removed either - that operation is replaceAll(",", "")'s job - and it does not count the columns for you: for that you take .length of the resulting array.

questions.prompt: The price column read from a CSV is in string form. What do Number("12.5") and Number("abc") return, respectively?

options.label: A
options.text: 12.5 and NaN

options.label: B
options.text: 12.5 and 0 - non-numeric strings are coerced to 0

options.label: C
options.text: 13 and NaN - Number rounds to the nearest integer

options.label: D
options.text: Both throw an error and stop the program

questions.explanation: When Number() can read the string as a number - decimals with a dot included - it returns that exact value, with no rounding whatsoever: Number("12.5") is 12.5 (rounding is Math.round's job). When it cannot, the result is NaN (*Not a Number*). The point most worth remembering for data work: NaN is not a program-stopping error - both calls run without incident, nothing is thrown - it just spreads silently into every calculation it touches (NaN + 5 is still NaN), so one "N/A" cell slipping into the price column turns the whole revenue total into NaN. That is why you check deliberately with Number.isNaN(value) right after converting. Nor does Number coerce broken strings to 0 (only the empty string "" gives 0 - a separate trap); if it did, things would actually be worse, because the total would still come out looking plausible.

questions.prompt: An order placed on March 10: what does new Date("2026-03-10T00:00:00").getMonth() return?

options.label: C
options.text: "March" - the month name as a string

questions.explanation: getMonth() counts months from 0: January is 0, March is 2, December is 11 - so a March order returns 2. The 3 your eye is waiting for is the trap itself: that is the month number as humans read it, not as getMonth counts it. The trap bites in both directions and produces no error message either way: filtering "March orders" must be written getMonth() === 2 (writing === 3 silently hands you April's data), while printing to a report requires adding 1 (getMonth() + 1) or every figure shifts back a month. Remember too that getMonth returns a number and never a month name as a string, while the 10 in the order date is what getDate() returns - the day of the month, which counts from 1 as normal (and do not confuse it with getDay() either - that is the day of the week). The inconsistency between the two counting rules is a legacy of the language you simply live with.

options.label: A
options.text: revenue

options.label: B
options.text: REVENUE - split runs first, so toLowerCase never gets applied

options.label: C
options.text: region

options.label: D
options.text: revenue - with two trailing spaces left over

questions.explanation: Follow the method chain left to right - the exact order of execution: trim() strips the whitespace from both ends of the whole string in the very first step, giving "Region,REVENUE"; toLowerCase() lowercases everything, giving "region,revenue"; split(",") cuts at the comma, giving the array ["region", "revenue"]; and columns[1] is the second element because indexes count from 0 - i.e. "revenue". There is no sense in which split "runs first" and robs toLowerCase of its chance: each method returns a new value and the next method runs on that value, so toLowerCase has finished with the whole string before split ever cuts it. Reading "region" out of this means counting indexes from 1 - the classic array beginner mistake, since "region" sits at columns[0]. As for the two trailing spaces, they belonged to the ends of the original whole string and trim() dealt with them at the start, before the string was ever cut into columns - none are left to cling to "revenue".

lessons.title: Reading error messages
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 51: Reading error messages

theory.contentHtml:
A revenue script gets halfway through the data and stops, leaving a wall of red text in the terminal. The reflex of most beginners is to scroll past it and start guessing where the code went wrong. But that wall already answers two questions: what happened, and where. This lesson teaches you to read it.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. The two parts of an error message
  2. The three error types you meet most
  3. Key points

1. The two parts of an error message

A typical JavaScript error message looks like this:

TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'region')

Read left to right, it has two parts:

  • The error type (TypeError) - tells you the category of the problem. JavaScript only has a handful; you will get to know their faces quickly.
  • The description (Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'region')) - tells you exactly what happened: the code was reading the property region off a value, and that value was undefined.

When running through Node or in the browser, a line number below points to the exact spot - the lesson "Reading errors and debugging with console" makes it the starting point of the debugging routine. The habit to build right now: do not skim past the red text. Beginners skip it and start guessing, throwing away two free answers.

2. The three error types you meet most

TypeError - a value is not the type the operation needs. The most common case: reading a property of undefined. The classic find example:

const orders = [{ id: 1, region: "north", amount: 1200000 }];
const order = orders.find((o) => o.id === 99);
console.log(order.region);
// TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'region')

When find matches nothing it returns undefined - and undefined.region is where things blow up. The error points at the console.log line, but the cause sits one line above: id 99 does not exist. That is an important lesson in itself: the reported line is where the error exploded, not necessarily where it started.

ReferenceError - a variable name that does not exist. The most common cause is a typo:

const revenue = 1200000;
console.log(revenu);
// ReferenceError: revenu is not defined

Read the description and you see it immediately: revenu is missing an e. When you see is not defined, the first move is to compare the name in the message with the name at the declaration.

SyntaxError - the code breaks the grammar, for example a missing bracket:

const amounts = [1200, 800, 600;
// SyntaxError: Unexpected token ';'

Unlike the other two, a SyntaxError happens before the program runs: JavaScript reads the whole file, sees broken grammar, and refuses to run even the first line. The next lesson explains why that puts a SyntaxError out of try/catch's reach.

Key points

An error message is two free answers. The type plus the description say "what"; the line number says "where". Read it before guessing.

The reported line is where the error exploded, not necessarily where it started. find returned undefined one line up; the TypeError detonated one line down.

Three names worth recognizing: TypeError (a value of the wrong type), ReferenceError (a variable name that does not exist, usually a typo), SyntaxError (broken grammar, raised before anything runs).

2. The three error types you meet most

lessons.title: trycatch and throw
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 52: trycatch and throw

theory.contentHtml:
Once you can read an error, the next question is whether the program should always crash. For bugs in your own logic it should - crash early, see it early, fix it early. But when 10,000 JSON lines arrive from another system and one truncated line takes down the whole pipeline, that is not acceptable. This lesson is the tool for the second situation.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. try/catch: catching instead of crashing
  2. Where to wrap: data outside your control
  3. throw: raising your own error on absurd input
  4. Key points

1. try/catch: catching instead of crashing

By default, a runtime error stops the program on the spot. try/catch gives you a second option: receive the error and decide what to do next.

try {
  const row = undefined;
  console.log(row.region);
} catch (err) {
  console.log("Something went wrong:", err.message);
}
console.log("Script is still running");
Something went wrong: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'region')
Script is still running

How to read it: the code inside try runs normally; if a line throws, the remaining lines in try are skipped and control jumps into catch. err is the error object, and err.message is exactly the description you learned to read in the previous lesson. After catch finishes, the program moves on - the last line still prints.

One limit worth knowing: try/catch only receives errors raised at run time. A SyntaxError happens before the program runs its first line, so no try block can reach it - fixing the grammar is the only way.

2. Where to wrap: data outside your control

Do not wrap try/catch around everything. Swallowing an error in your own logic lets a wrong number crawl quietly into a report, and costs you the very message that pointed at the broken spot. The places worth wrapping are where data you do not control enters the program.

The classic data case: reading JSON records from another system - an export from another tool, server logs, a file someone sent over. Out of thousands of lines one is truncated, and JSON.parse throws on a broken string:

const raw = '{"region":"central",';

try {
  const record = JSON.parse(raw);
  console.log("parsed:", record.region);
} catch (err) {
  console.log("broken record, skipped");
}

console.log("pipeline continues");
broken record, skipped
pipeline continues

Without try/catch, broken line number 4,213 takes down the whole run and you lose the 4,212 lines already processed. With it, the broken line is skipped and the rest moves on - and you even get a count of how many lines were dropped, a number worth logging in any real pipeline. The exercise right after this lesson has you turn that mechanism into a reusable function.

3. throw: raising your own error on absurd input

try/catch is the receiving end of errors; throw is the sending end. You use throw when your own function receives absurd input and you want to report it loudly instead of returning a silently wrong result:

function averageOrderValue(totalRevenue, orderCount) {
  if (orderCount === 0) {
    throw new Error("orderCount must be greater than 0");
  }
  return totalRevenue / orderCount;
}

try {
  console.log(averageOrderValue(9000000, 30));
  console.log(averageOrderValue(5000000, 0));
} catch (err) {
  console.log("Refused:", err.message);
}
300000
Refused: orderCount must be greater than 0

Why throw? Because JavaScript does not raise an error on division by zero - 5000000 / 0 returns Infinity, and Infinity will quietly flow through every later calculation into a meaningless report. throw new Error("...") turns absurd data into a loud, clear error with a description - exactly the kind of message you learned to read, except this time you wrote it.

As for finally: a finally block placed after catch always runs, error or not, and is meant for cleanup work. At this course's level you will rarely write one; you only need to recognize it in other people's code.

Key points

try/catch is for data outside your control, not for your own logic. Wrap the spot where another system's input gets read; let your own mistakes crash so you can see and fix them.

A SyntaxError cannot be caught with try/catch - it happens before the program runs. Fixing the grammar is the only way.

throw on absurd input. A silently wrong result (Infinity, NaN) is more dangerous than a loud, well-described error.

Count the records you drop. Skipping broken records without counting them hides how dirty your data actually is.

lessons.title: Reading errors and debugging with console
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 54: Reading errors and debugging with console

theory.contentHtml:
Errors that print red are the easy kind - they come with a message and a line number. The harder kind is a program that runs smoothly and produces the wrong number. This lesson gives you a three-step debugging routine that works for both, built on the tool you have used all course: console.log.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Start from the line number in the error
  2. console.log on intermediate values
  3. typeof when a type is suspect
  4. Silent errors: no crash, wrong result
  5. Key points

1. Start from the line number in the error

Run a script through Node and the error message comes with a full address:

report.js:12
  console.log(row.region);
                  ^
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'region')
    at report.js:12:19

report.js:12 means file report.js, line 12; 12:19 is line 12, column 19. Node even reprints the offending line with a ^ pointing at the exact spot. That is the starting point of the three-step routine:

  1. Read the line number in the message → open that line and look at which values are involved.
  2. console.log the intermediate values just before the failing line → find the first value that is "not what I thought".
  3. Narrow down: where did that broken value come from? Step back to where it was produced, log again, repeat until you reach the root.

The routine is boring - and precisely because it is boring, it still works when you are tired. Good debugging is not spotting bugs at a glance; it is shrinking the suspect area with discipline.

2. console.log on intermediate values

Two small techniques make console.log many times more useful. First, console.log takes multiple arguments - printed separated by spaces. Second, label each log call so you know which output line came from where:

const rows = [
  { region: "north", amount: 1200000 },
  { region: "south", amount: 800000 },
  { region: "north", amount: 600000 },
];

const filtered = rows.filter((r) => r.region === "north");
console.log("after filter:", filtered);

const total = filtered.reduce((sum, r) => sum + r.amount, 0);
console.log("total:", total);
after filter: [
  {
    "region": "north",
    "amount": 1200000
  },
  {
    "region": "north",
    "amount": 600000
  }
]
total: 1800000

When total comes out wrong, the after filter: log tells you immediately which half to look at: if the filtered array is already wrong, the problem is in the filter condition; if the array is right but the sum is wrong, the problem is in reduce. One well-placed log line cuts the suspect area in half - that is the whole spirit of step 2.

Without labels, the output is just bare values stacked on each other, and you will waste time guessing which line belongs to which log - making things harder for yourself exactly when you need a clear head most.

3. typeof when a type is suspect

A great many data bugs reduce to one question: is this value a number or a string? typeof answers in one line:

const amountFromCsv = "1200000";
console.log(typeof amountFromCsv, amountFromCsv);
console.log(typeof Number(amountFromCsv), Number(amountFromCsv));
string 1200000
number 1200000

The two output lines look almost identical - only the leading string/number differs - but that difference decides whether + means addition or string concatenation. Data read from CSV, from user input, from URLs is always a string until you convert it yourself; when a calculation produces something bizarre, running typeof on the inputs is the fastest test there is.

4. Silent errors: no crash, wrong result

The most expensive class of bug in data work prints no red text at all. The program runs to completion, exits cleanly - and returns the wrong number. Two familiar culprits:

NaN propagation. Number("abc") does not throw; it returns NaN, and NaN combined with anything through any arithmetic gives NaN:

const amounts = ["1200000", "abc", "800000"];
const total = amounts.reduce((sum, text) => sum + Number(text), 0);
console.log("total:", total);
total: NaN

One broken value in the middle of the array poisons the entire sum. When NaN shows up in a final result, do not stare at the last line - log each value after conversion to find the first element that became NaN. To make the program defend itself, filter with Number.isNaN before summing - the exercise right after this lesson makes you do exactly that.

Comparing strings while thinking they are numbers. Two strings compare in dictionary order, character by character:

const a = "900000";
const b = "1200000";
console.log("as strings:", a > b);
console.log("as numbers:", Number(a) > Number(b));
as strings: true
as numbers: false

"900000" > "1200000" is true because the character "9" sorts after "1" - done, the rest is never looked at. The program does not crash, the comparison "works", except 900 thousand is now greater than 1.2 million. Sort revenue figures without converting first and this is exactly the leaderboard you get.

Key points

The three-step routine: read the line number → log intermediate values → narrow down. Boring, but it works when you are tired - debugging is discipline, not intuition.

Log with labels and multiple arguments: console.log("after filter:", rows). Unlabeled output makes things harder for yourself.

typeof is the fastest test when a type is suspect. Data from CSV/input/URLs is a string until you convert it yourself.

Silent errors cost more than red ones. NaN propagation and string comparison are the two familiar culprits - both "work", both produce wrong results.

Specific to this course's practice exercises: after debugging, DELETE every leftover console.log before submitting. Grading compares your output character by character - one leftover debug line makes the output differ from the expected answer, and the submission fails even with correct logic.

lessons.title: JavaScript charting libraries
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 56: JavaScript charting libraries

theory.contentHtml:
The number one reason data people touch JavaScript: interactive charts on the web. A PNG exported from Python is a dead image; a JavaScript chart runs right in the browser - hover to see values, click to filter, embed it in a dashboard the whole team can open without installing anything. This lesson walks through the three names you will meet. Every code block illustrates an external library - reading them is enough; they cannot run on this page.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Chart.js: describe the chart with an object
  2. D3: assemble graphics from primitives
  3. Observable: notebooks for JavaScript
  4. Key points

1. Chart.js: describe the chart with an object

Chart.js is the easiest way in: you describe the chart with a configuration object and it handles the drawing.

new Chart(ctx, {
  type: "bar",
  data: {
    labels: ["North", "South", "Central"],
    datasets: [{ label: "Revenue (VND)", data: [1800000, 1400000, 900000] }],
  },
});

Look closely at the data part: the labels are an array of strings, the values an array of numbers - exactly the structures you have used all course. Real work with Chart.js is mostly turning raw data into those two arrays, which means map/filter/reduce, not drawing skills.

2. D3: assemble graphics from primitives

D3 sits at the other end of the scale: there are no prebuilt "chart types"; you assemble graphics from primitive elements and control every detail.

d3.select("svg")
  .selectAll("rect")
  .data([1800000, 1400000, 900000])
  .join("rect");

Most of the beautiful custom charts on major news sites (New York Times, Reuters) are built with D3. The learning path is considerably longer than Chart.js - the pragmatic advice: start with Chart.js, and only move to D3 when your customization needs outgrow what Chart.js offers.

3. Observable: notebooks for JavaScript

If you know Jupyter, Observable (observablehq.com) is its JavaScript relative: a notebook where you write and run JS right in the browser, cell by cell, results appearing instantly - nothing to install. It is the ideal place to practice charts: most official D3 examples live on Observable, where you can open one, edit the numbers, and watch the picture change.

One difference from Jupyter worth knowing upfront: Observable cells re-run automatically based on their dependencies - change one value and every cell that uses it updates, closer to a spreadsheet than to a top-down notebook.

Key points

All three consume arrays and objects. This course's skills are the entry ticket: the real work is shaping raw data into the form the library expects, not learning to draw.

Chart.js first, D3 later. Chart.js trades flexibility for speed by giving you prebuilt chart types; move to D3 only when your customization needs outgrow that.

Observable is the cheapest place to experiment. Nothing to install and the official D3 examples are already there - just remember its cells re-run by dependency, not top to bottom like Jupyter.

lessons.title: Node, npm and where to go next
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 57: Node, npm and where to go next

theory.contentHtml:
This course taught you the core of JavaScript: variables, functions, arrays of objects, and the map/filter/reduce trio. The final theory lesson answers the remaining question: where else this code runs besides the browser, and where to go next from this foundation.

📑 Lesson contents:

  1. Node.js and npm: JavaScript outside the browser
  2. fetch and async/await: the next step
  3. How much JavaScript do data people need
  4. Key points

1. Node.js and npm: JavaScript outside the browser

JavaScript was born in the browser, but it is not locked in there. Node.js is a runtime that runs JavaScript like any ordinary scripting language - reading files, writing files, running from the terminal:

node report.js

The practice exercises in this very course are graded by running your code exactly that way. For data people, Node is useful when you need a script that processes JSON/CSV files living in the same repo as a JavaScript dashboard - one language for both the processing and the display.

Alongside Node comes npm - the JavaScript community's library registry, the equivalent of Python's pip. Installing a CSV parsing library, for instance:

npm install papaparse

then using it in a script:

const Papa = require("papaparse");
const parsed = Papa.parse(csvText, { header: true });
console.log(parsed.data);

In the upcoming capstone you will parse CSV by hand with split - worth doing once to understand the mechanics, but in real work, where data is dirty in every way imaginable (commas inside quotes, BOMs, encodings), use a library that has been patched through thousands of cases, like Papa Parse.

2. fetch and async/await: the next step

Read JavaScript in the wild and you will soon meet this shape:

const response = await fetch("https://api.example.com/orders");
const orders = await response.json();
console.log(orders.length);

fetch calls an API over the network to pull data in; await belongs to the async/await syntax - JavaScript's way of handling operations that must wait (network, files) without freezing the whole program.

This course stops at synchronous code on purpose - everything you learned runs top to bottom with no waiting. That is not a gap but the right learning order: async/await is worth learning when you have a real need to call an API for data, and at that point the hard part is not the syntax but the mindset of "the result is not here yet". Every array skill from this course keeps its full value - once the data fetched arrives, the remaining work is still map/filter/reduce.

3. How much JavaScript do data people need

The short answer: you do not need to become a frontend developer. React, CSS, state management - that is a different profession. What data people need is two far more modest things:

  • Read and understand a piece of JavaScript when you meet one: the Chart.js config in your team's dashboard, a tracking script a web developer wrote, a D3 example on Observable.
  • Write a compact data-processing passage: take an array of records, clean it, group it, total it, and shape it into exactly what a charting library expects.

Both stand on the foundation you just finished. A Chart.js configuration is just an object nesting arrays; an Observable example is just chained map/filter calls. The hardest part of "JavaScript for data people" - modeling data as arrays of objects and the habit of transforming them step by step - is already behind you.

Key points

Node is JavaScript outside the browser, npm is JavaScript's pip. One language usable for both the processing script and the dashboard that displays it.

Parse CSV by hand to understand, use a library to work. Real data is dirtier than exercises; Papa Parse and friends have patched thousands of cases you have not met yet.

Stopping at synchronous code is deliberate. async/await + fetch is the next step, once you have a real need to call an API - nothing you learned needs relearning.

No need to become a frontend dev. Reading JS and writing short data-processing passages - those two are enough, and you have the foundation for both.

lessons.title: Quiz Course wrap-up
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 59: Quiz Course wrap-up

questions.prompt: Throughout this course you declared variables mostly with const. When do you actually need let?

options.label: A
options.text: When the variable holds a number or a string - const is only for arrays and objects

options.label: B
options.text: When you need to assign a NEW value to the variable after declaring it - for example an accumulator or a counter in a loop

options.label: C
options.text: When the variable is an object, because const makes the object's properties unchangeable

options.label: D
options.text: Never - let is old syntax that const has replaced

questions.explanation: const forbids exactly one thing: reassignment - writing x = ... a second time. The signal that you need let is therefore very concrete: the code contains a second assignment to the same name, like let total = 0; followed by total += amount; inside a loop - that is (b). (a) is wrong because const works for every kind of value; numbers and strings are perfectly normal. (c) is wrong in the opposite direction: const does NOT lock the contents - const rows = [] still allows rows.push(...); the only thing forbidden is assigning rows to a different array. That is the most common misunderstanding about const. (d) is wrong because let is modern syntax - the thing considered obsolete is var; let remains necessary whenever you genuinely must reassign.

questions.prompt: Which of the following expressions evaluates to true?

options.label: B
options.text: 0 === false

options.label: C
options.text: Number("5") === 5

options.label: D
options.text: "" === false

questions.explanation: === compares without type coercion: both sides must have the same type AND the same value. (c) is true because Number("5") returns the number 5, and 5 === 5 is two equal numbers. (a) is false because one side is a string and the other a number - === returns false the moment the types differ, however alike they "look". (b) and (d) share the same trap: 0 and "" are both falsy values, but falsiness only matters when a value gets coerced to boolean in a condition (if (x)); it does not make 0 (a number) or "" (a string) equal to false (a boolean) under === - different types means false, no further checking needed.

options.label: A
options.text: 8 then 8

options.label: B
options.text: 8 then undefined

options.label: C
options.text: undefined then 8

options.label: D
options.text: An error, because the function has no return

questions.explanation: Calling double(4): the console.log(x * 2) inside the function prints 8 - the first output. But the function has no `return`, so the expression double(4) evaluates to undefined, and result receives undefined - the last line prints undefined, giving (b). (a) confuses the course's core distinction between printing and returning: console.log only puts text on screen for a human to read; it does not hand a value out of the function for code to use. (c) has the order backwards - the print inside the function runs before the assignment completes. (d) is wrong because a function without return is perfectly legal in JavaScript; it simply returns undefined. The course-long lesson: to use a result further, the function must return it; console.log is for human eyes only.

questions.prompt: You have an array orders, each element an object { id, region, amount }. Your boss needs ONE single number: the total amount across all orders. Which tool fits the job?

options.label: A
options.text: map - transform each order and take the result

options.label: B
options.text: filter - pick the orders that have an amount and take the result

options.label: C
options.text: reduce - fold the whole array into one accumulated value

options.label: D
options.text: sort - sort by amount and take the last element

questions.explanation: Pick the tool by the shape of the result: the input is an array of N elements, the output must be ONE value - that is exactly reduce's job, with an accumulator starting at 0 and each step adding one order's amount: (c). (a) is wrong because map always returns an array of the same length as the input - it transforms each element but folds nothing; after map you still hold N unadded values. (b) is wrong because filter returns a subset of the array - it selects elements by a condition and computes nothing on them. (d) is wrong because sort only reorders; the last element after sorting is the LARGEST order, not the total. The quick mnemonic: reshape each element → map; pick a subset → filter; array down to one value → reduce.

options.label: C
options.text: NaN

options.label: D
options.text: An error, because a string cannot be added to a number

questions.explanation: split always returns an array of strings - parts[1] is the string "1200000", not a number, however number-like it looks. When either side of + is a string, + becomes string concatenation: "1200000" + 500000 gives "1200000500000" - printed as (b). (a) is the business-correct result, but only reachable after converting first: Number(parts[1]) + 500000 is what gives 1700000 - the mandatory ritual when parsing CSV. (c) is wrong because NaN only appears when a numeric conversion fails (like Number("abc")); there is no conversion here, only concatenation. (d) is wrong because JavaScript raises no error when adding a string to a number - it silently concatenates, and that very silence is what makes this class of bug dangerous: the program runs smoothly, the result is wrong.

Walk it stage by stage, like real debugging. Stage 1 - filter keeps the orders with region === "north": 2 orders remain, amounts 1200 and 600. Stage 2 - reduce starts with sum = 0 and accumulates: 0 + 1200 = 1200, then 1200 + 600 = 1800 - printing (b). (a) 3100 is the total of ALL FOUR orders - what you get by forgetting the filter or assuming it does nothing; wrong because the south/central orders were dropped before the summing. (c) 2 is the COUNT of orders after filtering - confusing counting with summing; this reduce adds o.amount, it does not count elements. (d) 1200600 is string concatenation - it would only happen if amount were a string or the seed were ""; here amount is a number and the seed is the number 0, so + is genuine addition. This question packs the skeleton of the whole course: data as an array of objects, a subset chosen with filter, folded into one number with reduce.
